CLEAR ideas on this subject are of such vast
importance to the workmen, that I shall offer
no excuse for adding yet a few words to the
friendly discussion between Mr. LLOYD JONES
and myself.
It can hardly be necessary for me to repeat
for the third time that I look on the" stores"
as invaluable institutions, and on productive
Co-operation as a most valuable experiment. I
expect great things yet from the stores, and
wish every success to the producing societies.
My warning, however, was not to expect too
much. What I say is, that Co-operation is in
no position to transform tho whole conditions
of industry, and to give us a new social future.
Mr. LLOYD JONES now asks me, as I under-
stand, who ever said that it would? To which
I answer by referring him to recent articles
in the BEE-HIVE. For instance, Dr. TRAVIS,
who has every right to be heard, tells us, in
the 131m-IlivE of October 26th, that Co-
operation is employed in two different senses.
." Ii One sense it means merely trading Co-
operation in the nzidst of all the social abomi-
nations of 11th existing system," ° he other,
he says, is "Social Co-operation, the system
of which ROBERT OwEN was the founder."
Thus, according to Dr. TRAVIS, that kind of
Co-operation which is not 'social, and founded
on Owenistn, leaves all the existing social
abominations. Clearly, then, Dr. Tulvis
would agree with me in calling Co-operation a
form of socialism, and he distinctly looks to it
as a means of superseding the relation of em-
ployer and employed. Anything which does
not do this he looks on as merely the old social
abomination.

I certainly gather the same thing from Mr.
LLOYD JONES' own remarks last week and at
other times. He also looks forward, it ap-
pears, to a time when the " co-operative
voice" shall say to the workmen "let us

depart hence ; ho our own employers, and ours
the capital which supplies wages. That
implies an entirely different distribution of
wealth ,and different relations of labour to capital.
But a plan of society with a now distribution
of wealth, and new relations of industry is
usually called socialism, and I use it in no
hostile sense. Of course, as Mr. Um%) JONES
supposes, I never for one moment imputed
any forcible retribution of wealth to any
school. But when he asks me where I find
such a theory put forward as the true meaning
of Co-operation, I ask him to listen to Dr.
TRANI%

Now, when Co-operation uses the language
of socialism, or when its voico is herd saying
to the workmen "lot us depart hence," I
think reflecting men will very distinctly put
to it the question, "Whore are we going to ?"
Do you v. ish to make workman and capitalist,

employer and employed, convertible terms,
applying equally to one and the same person;
and in superseding the existing method of em-
ployment, what exactly do you substitute for
it? A new mode of buying candles and soap
may be a very good thing, but it will not do
away with the "existing social abominations."
If we are to have a revision of the actual
relations of society, lot us know exactly what
the new ones are to be. Owenism, Fourierism,
and the other schemes very definitely worked
out their own programmes. I cannot find that
Co-operation has ever done this. It appears
to mean a dozen differeu% things according to
the speaker. We ought to know exactly what
is orthodox Co-operation. Dr. TlitiVlS says it
is an improved Owenista ; others say it con-
sists in teaching working men to save; Mr.
LLOYD JONES says that it means "let us
depart hence." Which is its true form, the
purely economical or the semi-socialistic?

To illustrate this in details, wages are now
determined by supply and demand; i.e., no
employer gives higher wages than the market
rate. Now, in " Co-operation," will the
association give higher wages than the market
rate, or, what is the same thing, a bonus on
the wages paid? If it does not, then surely
Co-operation is to everyone but those who own
the shares competition over again. If it does
do this, then on what rate are the wages or
bonus paid? By what principle is this to be
determined? Again, in buying and selling
stock, are the Co-operators to follow market
rates, and if not, why not? What share does
lie who lends:his savings, i.e., the equivalent
of fast labour, and he who gives his labour
rightly, take in the joint produce? What is
the principle which deoides the relative value
of capital and labour? Again, if the profits
are largely diverted to extra wages to labour,
will tho capital grow, that is to say, will a
thriving business be done? And if one of the
great objeots is to hold out inducements to
accumulate savings, this will not be promoted
by a system which diminishes the profits of
savings. Let us assume that 100,000 work-
men have each saved £lOO which they invest
in Co-operative mills; will they continue to be
workmen themselves, and if so, why should
they? And will they pay the workmen
they employ higher wages than their
neighbours do, and if so, why should they?
The 000nom1111 section of Co-operators
will be scandalised by a proposal to throw
the support of those who do not save on
those who do, and thus diminish the incentive
to saving. Why are these 100,000 workmen,
who have atoll saved £lOO to be as employers,
so superior to the 1,000 or so of workmen who
constantly are rising into the capitalist
class ?

As a matter of fact, there is no doctrine
accepted amongst Co-operators as the true
one. These points are discussed from
the most opposite points of view, yet
they are the essential ,principles on which
it must stand or fall. In practice, the purely
economical school carry their point; and al-
most all the existing co-operative manufac-
tunics proceed on the rule of competition, so
far as the men employed in them are con-
cerned. Mr. Lr.ovn JONES has been, he tel!s
us, connected with Co-operation since 1832.
Yet he can hardly point to an example of the
contrary. He condemns one form of it, and
deplores another. And after forty years, Co-
operation has not yet entered on the true path

as he understands it, After an experience of
forty years, what number of co-operative
societies are paying the workmen they employ
anything more than the current rates of
wages? And what number of workmen are
now employed by such societies genuinely
owned by working men who are paid more
than the market rates? Mr. LLorn JONES
has not answered this question.
There is always the distributive side of Co-
operation—that:is, the stores. Much as I value
it, I cannot look on it as the gigantic engine of,
the future that Mr. LLOYD JONES believes it to
be. Heirputs the case of the co-operative busi-
ness done by the wages classes at £100,000,000,
on which he calculates a profit of £15,000,000
per annum. But by what miracle are the
working classes of the country to become com-
petent to manage a business of £100,000,000
per annum, in addition to their daily work,
with an average profit of 15 per cent.? The
trading classes, accustomed to business all
their lives, have never learnt this art. Of 1
the vast sums devoted to railways, banks, and
insurances, an immense proportion is lost;
and perhaps half of it scarcely earns 2 per
amt. The sixteen millions sunk in the
Chatham and Dover Railway does not return
16 per cent. Why are working men's " stores "
to be exempt from Chatham and Dover
smashes? Large sums have been invested by
the working class in insurance societies, but
frightful losses and mismanagement have been
discovered in many of them. One of the '
ablest workmen I ever knew told me once, in
talking of his " store," that he understood all
about his own chisel, -but that he knew very
little about buying cheese, Small clubs to
purchase the necessaries of life may be most
useful in their way; but long before the
leisure-hour trading of working men had
reached £100,.000,000 a year, there would have
been some tremendous smashes, and wide-
spread loss. Work of every kind, bricklaying,
choose-buying, trading, or banking requires
special training, and practice. And
there is no magic existing by means of which
working men can undertake the duties of every
class in the community simply by covering
them under the elastic phrase of Co-operation.

It is quite needless to continue this dis-
cussion at length, and I will only point out
that I think Mr. LLOYD .Tos has been a
little betrayed into an obvious fallacy. An
increased production of 60 per cent, in any
particular factory, is a very different thing
from that increase of production over the
entire trade. I said, any firm who adopted
the relay system might, with their existing
machinery, add 60 per cent, to their produc-
tion. But I did not say that all firms would
do it together. On the contrary, those who
delayed would be prevented from want of
men. As to reducing the number of firms, of
course that, like any:other economic change,
would come about voluntarily, under the very
simple plan of going into partnership. if
ABCD now employ each 100 men in four
different works, it would be a very natural
thing for A B and Co., and for C D and Co. to
employ each 200 men in two different works,
As to Mr. LLOYD JONES' horror of these
colossi, I eannot_understand it. All and Co.
would not be more formidable than A and B.
Indeed, by the assumption, tho now firm
would not need a very muoh increased capital,
but their workmen are doubled. If the capital
even were doubled ,still the workmen are doubled

too in every set of works. If 100 men in a
Workshop or a factory are now able to hold
their own pretty well, why are they likely to
be "hopelessly crushed down" when there are
200 in the same workshop? This, I confess,
puzzles me. If the capitalists under the relay
system become in any new sense colossi, it is
because they would employ more workmen.
And the men would thus be stronger 100 per
cent. ,

NEW LIGHT.

AMONGST the many things it is said working
men ought to turn their attention to, the ques-
tion of Coolie traffic and slavery in Africa
should be ranked as of very high importance.
Political power possessed by workers should
be used for the protection of labour wherever
it suffers wrong, espeoially where that wrong
is of such a character as to be an outrage on
humanity as well as on justice and right.
What has been suffered by the workers of the
past not be recalled only so far as it may

on, each other in pursuit of personal gain.
Those who know anything of the old African

were heaped together in the holds of accursed

as a plague the poor creatures confined in such

Working men in England now consider their

DEATH IN THE MINE.

GRIM Death has three famous allies in our
growing civilisation: accidents on railways;
disasters by sea; anii catastrophes in mines.
These appear to be the Juggernauts of seisms,

t differ in this, that whereas the votaries of
VISITSIT were the offerings of ignorant
devotees, the victims above referred to are not.
The mangled, and dead which annually swell
this great army of martyrs are enough to make
one shudder at the cheapness of human life.
We too often look abroad for objects of pity
when they lie plentifully enough at our own
doors. "The death march of India" "touched
a- chord of infinite fibre," which vibrated
throughout the land; and a massacre in New
Zealand sends a thrill of horror into many a
peaceful home.
When a railwey.aecident occurs, resulting
in loss of life, the ghastly annals harrow the
feelings
,ef tens of thousands who read the
eicikening tale. If a ship is wrecked along our
dangerous shores universal pity is felt fm the
poor sailor, tat it cannot be denied that
the greatest consternation is felt at railway
accidents; this comes from the fact that all of
, us are more or less travellers, but we are not
all sailors; and moreover that the former
occur Most frequently from preventible causes.
A consideration of the facts connected
with the terrible sacrifice of life in the calami-
ties named, will, show; most incontestibly that
of all these the miners are the greatest suf-
ferers.

, The time is opportune for the discussion of
I this question, inasmuch as we have had. all
three of these forms of death before our eyes,
through the daily papers, during the past week
or two, such as the Alorley Alain Mine explo-
sion,,the railway accident at liirtlebridge, and
the disasters along our coast during the recent
gales, la addition to which some returns
rpoently issued will assist us in the comparisons
we-Assize to make,
. _ _

The total loss of life on the railways of the
United Kingdom last year was 404, out of a
total of 307,000,000 passengers and 200,000
employees, or a total of 307,200,000 persons,
being one in 760,396. There were also 1,261
Injured, being one in 243,809. But of those
killed 16, were suicideb, and 77 trespassers,
neither of which can rightly be charged as
accidents in the ordinary sense. Of the killed
and injured, railway servants form a large pro-
portion, being one in 1,740 killed, and one in
1,560 injured.
The less of life by shipping disasters around
our coasts and surrounding seas, during the
past year, was 626-131 of which are stated to
have 'been the result of carelessness, and
similar causes. The proportion of losses to
persons I have not at hand. Here then we
have a total loss of life by railway aooideetts
and casualties by sea, of 1,030.
Let us compare the dad havoc, to human life
by these two engines of death to the terrible
mining accidents which so frequently occur,
and we shall find that the loss of life in our
mines during the past year was 1,075, out of a
total employed of 370,881 persons, or one life
sacrificed to every 345 employed. For the
ten years ending 1870 one life was lost in
every 300 employed; for the ten years pre-
ceding that, one to every 245.
The deaths in coal mines alone, during
twenty years-1851 to 1870 inclusive—were
20,644 persons; in addition to which, the
deaths in our iron stone mines, number about
68 per annum, bringing up the sad total to
over 22,000 persons. In addition, however,
to this ghastly list, there are about 10,500
accidents to persons every year, some 6,000 of
which are of such a character, that those
so injured are never fully restored to health—
a large proportion being rendered blind, lame,
or so 'pained, that they are unable to follow
their ordinary employments ever afterwards.
So that not only have we one death in every
345 employed, but one in every 354 is
more or less injured.

The facts here disclosed are so startling and
sad, that your indulgence is craved to place
them before the public, to the end that some
means might be devised to shield these workers
in the cold darleraine from some of the hard-
ships to which they are liable in their daily
occupations, or to take some steps to befriend
those injured for life, and to provide for the
fatherless and the widow, who are deprived of
their means of living by the sad fate of
husbands and fathers when toiling to provide
for us the greatest boon to our country, a good
supply of coal and iron.

Our National Life-boat Institution looks
after the poor sailor, our courts of law com-
pensate the railway traveller,but the poor miner,
as a rule, is left to his own resources, and to
the generous aid of his own co-workers.

GEORGE HOWELL.

A GOVERNMENT CRIIIE.

GAMBLING is an indictable offence by our
law. When two or more persons agree and
confederate together to commit such an offence,
It is a conspiracy at common law. The Go-
vernment of Hong-Kong has been licensing
gambling-hells, and putting up gambling
licenses for sale by public auction! The
question, therefore, arises of whether this con-
stitutes an offence pinishable by our English
courts of law, and which I hope they may
have to decide. The following document ap-
peared in the Times of last Saturday. The
docuMent speaks for itself:—

articles.title: GOVERNMENT NOTIFICATION.
articles.text:
GOVERNMENT NOTIFICATION.

In reference to Government Notification No.
149, of the 23rd November, 1870, notice is hereby
given that the gaming-house licenses will be put
up to auction, in lieu of ,the
.drawing of lots,
at 2 p.m. on the 12th inst., at the Government
offices.
The conditions under which the auction will be
held are hereunto annexed.
By Command,
J. GARDINER AUSTIN, Colonial Secretary,
Colonial Secretary's Office, Hong-Kong, Jan.
6, 1871.

I need not tell working men that this is au
odioua iniquity on the part of our authorities.
Can nobody be made answerable for it? How
Thug ha a this been known to the Government
in London? What steps have they taken to
stop it; or have they winked at it and let it go
on? I hope that some member of Parliament
will take the matter up and insist upon a full
inquiry, and punishment of the guilty—
although inquiry by the House of Commons is
rather a hopeless business; for each person,
who ought to be held answerable, kfiows how
to shift the responsibility off his own sheulders;
and even if a good deal of smoke is made at
first about such an affair 'as this, it is all
smoke and nothing else. There occur delays
and puttings-off—influence here and wire-pull-
ing there—and in the end it is all right for
everybody. It is all nicely hushed up and
smoothed over. In our mode of government
the official wriggling-out of crimes and messes
is cultivated as a fine art. Oh, for responsi-
bility without talk, instead of talk without re-
ponsibility. But, perhaps, if the matter ever
does come before the House of Commons, we
shall be treated to high-sounding , speeches of
the usual length, to gull us into the belief that
it is not so alter all, and that our senses have
deceived us; or perhaps we may be told that
gambling is good for the Chinese, just in the
same way as when Mr. GLAIMIONE and Mr.
GRANT Dun?, with huge audacity, defended
the compulsory opium trade, which we forced
upon China, by asserting that the daily use of
opium as an article of everyday consumption
was beneficial and healthy for the Chinese.
The physician who sees a spot upon his
patient can often tell the nature of the disease
from which the man is suffering. This gam-
bling system, this sale of ganaisling licenses by
public auction, is a , plague spot, a symptom
which cannot be mistaken. it indicates the
diseased condition of our official life in the
East, which, in its turn, springs from the total
absence of all morality in our international life
in our conduct towards other nations. I have
narrated at length in these columns the history
of the crimes which the English Government
has committed in China, how many of these
crimes were to be attributed to the misgovern-
ment of Hong-Kong, and to the entire absence
of a code of morals to direct our national eon-
duet. This gambling system clearly indicates
that the same ignoble view and low state of
public morality still exist out in the East—
that the requisite moral and intellectual changs
in official lire and policy has not yet taken
place. Whose fault is this? Whose fault, I
ask, is it that gambling-hells have been licensed
in tho British Empire—or that such an occur-
rence is possible? This, then, is the last new
thing from our immaculate Government, which
is always so horror-struck at everything done -
by other people, which is so roady to exact

hars-h penal law fl against other classes, and
yet which never sees its own misdeeds. I Wol2'
der What next?

HENRY CROMPTON.

. . .
EDUCATION FOR THE NEW SYSTEM.

A FRIEND has written to me to ask for an
exact description in the BEE-HIVE of the waY
in which the knowledge of the causes of evil
and of good will operate to produce the trans-
formation of character which is necessary for,
the realization of the Co-operative Social
System. He does not yet see it. I will try
to enable him to do so, hoping that other
readers also may be interested. For this is
the key to the new system. To imagine, as
not a few do, that the co-operative state of
society can be realised without the co-operative
character is as unwise as it would be to
imagine that a man might paint an artistic)
picture without any knowledge of drawing.
For the realization of this system it is neces-
sary that men—those, at least, who are to be
instrumental as leaders in introducing it—
should acquire a character of true enlighten-
ment and.enlightened goodness, instead of the
very defective intellectual and moral character
which all, of every class, have hitherto been
caused to acquire. Those who are not leaders
may acquire the new character within the' new
influences; and
,all children educated within
them will be caused to acquire it as naturally
as all in the present system are caused to

articles.title: OUR FOREIGN POLICY.
articles.text:
OUR FOREIGN POLICY.

WE have no wish to occupy your space
with any exhaustive disquisition on
foreign policy of Great Britain, but perhaps
it might be desirable, in the present critical
conjuncture of
.affsirs, to impress upon your
readers the absolute necessity of forming clear
definite conceptions of the attitude we. ought
to assume towards Continental Powers. In a
former article we attempted to reason out the
propriety of contracting a defensive and, under
certain favourable conditions, an offensive
alliance • with France. Those hypothetical
stipulations were that nothing should be ar-
ranged until France had honourably paid up
the whole of the war indemnity; that, at
least, five or six years should be suffered to
elapse, in order to give ample
;time for, the
effective development of her new system of
military discipline and scientific education,
and, one may add, for the ripening into man-
hood of the youthful heroes
.who fought so
gallantly under the standards of CHAM)
FAIDEERDE, and D'AURELLE DE PA.LADINE ;
that, moreover, with due regard for eouteraet-
ing considerations, such as the overpowering
motive of self-preservation, no assistance
should be proffered, unless by treaty we had
previously secured the neutrality of Russia
and Austria; that, after the expulsion of the
Germans from Alsace-Lorraine, terms of peace
should be proposed on the basis of all parties
retaining such territories as each possessed
previous to the Treaty of Versailles.

We then advocated what perhaps may .not
inappropriately be termed a high moral pru-
dential anti-German war policy. We are now
anxious to caution your readers, especially
those who belong to the upper classes, against
the folly and wickedness either of harbouring
resentful feelings against America, or of in-
dulging in a by ne moans harnileas fit Of
Itnasiti-phebic. It would, lu'very truth', be eri.
minal foflytodöoltr sa against a
Power like the United States, which, with all its
faults, has done so much for the cause of
human freedom, and human] happiness, and
with whom we are bound by so many endear-
ing ties of race, kindred, and mutual peaceful
agitation for noble political aims. We un-
hesitatingly aver that, for the sake of preserv-
ing amicable and conciliatory relations towards
our Americaik• cousins, and husbanding all
our resources- for a struggle with Prussia, we
might patiently endure humiliations far more
grievous than are involved in an adverse deci-
sion respecting trumpery boundaries, or the
loss of a few millions on amount of the dis-
reputable practices of a Tory mercantile firm.
Peace at almost any price should be the key-
stone of our policy in that part of the world.
Nor indeed is it at all advisable that we
should try to prevent the advance of the
:Romanoffs in Central Asia. Doubtless official
traditions point towards a policy of interference,
but the arguments against it are conclusive.
In the first place the Cabinet of St. Petersburg
has legitimate grounds of complaint against
this savage KaaN of jcuiv.t, who, it appears,
has an objectionable habit of kidnapping Rus-
sian citizens, and, of course, subjecting them to
all manner of hardships. Secondly, human
interests are paramount to those of petty ill
conducted barbaric nationalities, the extinetion
of which cannot but conduce to the general
welfare of mankind. Besides, in accordance
with the law of natural selection, the superior

Caudasiin race is destined to cOratinuts its
career of supplanting svith as much gentleness
as is compatible with conquest, the Turanian
or Mongol aborigines. Now it so happens that
the Russian advance, avoiding Persia, the
denizens of which are Caucasian, seeks to
extend itself along a line running in a south-
easterly direction from the southern extremity
of the Caspian sea, as far as the Hindoo Koosh
mountains, the whole of the districts they
wish to conquer being inhabited by Mongols.
Setting apart a strip of territory, 400 miles in
extent, lying- between the above mentioned
mountain range and our Indian possessions,
which if occupied by Russia might possibly
turn out to be a source of danger, but the dis-
posal of which may be safely relegated to the
diplomacy of Lord GRANVILLE'S successor, it
is enough for the present to protest against
any silly ill-judged meddling with indisputable
natural laws. Ever since the dispersion at
Shiner, the JAPHETITE and the &MINUTE have
been gradually enlarging their doruinions,
driving before them, and-either exterminating,
or incorporating into their own political
system, the native inhabitants. The subjuga-
tion by Russia of tribes hopelessly destitute of
all civilizing influences, but at the same time
of extensive and fertile districts susceptible of
indefinite cultivation, may be defended, as
being desirable, not only in the interests of
commerce, but in the interests of the natives
themselves, who in this manner alone can he
purified of their many deeply-ingrained evil
habits. Is not this new migration of—the
Caucasian race an unerring indication of the
beneficent designs of the Supreme Architect,
who thus now, as in times gone by, visibly
works out the fulfilment of His grand civilizing
purpose through natural means?
Lord. NORTHEROOIt then has acted very
wisely, in refusing poinb blank to protect the
Kress of Kurva. There is really no danger
either now or at any future period of Russia
striving to conquer India. For many years to
come, the function she has assumed of sub-
duing and humanizing the semi-barbarous
peoples between the Aral Sea and the lihirgis
Steppes on the one side, and Afghanistan and
Surinam on the other, is one that will task
some of her best energies. And afterwards it
will manifestly be to her interest to make a
friendly agreement with England as to the
disposition of the tracts bordering on our
Indian Empire. But even if it were desirable
to check Russia, it is evident that we have not
the power to do so. Suppose we sent troops to
help the KHtN, no success that might bald
our arms could be more than temporary. Our
blood and treasures would be expended to no
purpose. Probably we should be afterwards
attacked by the very persons who had invoked
odr assistance, intercepted in the rear by bands
of hostile saVages, all means of retreat through
mountain defiles would be out off, and not a
trade left of the ill-starred Khiva Expedi-
tion

No; the time has now arrived for a distinct
recognition of the expediency of regulating
our external intervention by a diligent study
of the higher mental and moral laws of nature.
These laws, like the ones governing the
change of the seasons, or the flight of birds, or
the
.revolutions of the planets, are continually
acting and reacting upon each other. Con-
siderations—moral, political, and commercial
—being gravely weighed in the balance, the
resultant of such deliberations must embody
itself in an enlightened foreign policy. Our
demeanour towards foreign States must ulti-
lnately depend upon the degree of weight to
be attached to a number of powerful, and it
it may be conflicting forces, one of which,
taken singly, might lead us astray, but which,
when', sifted, analysed, and combined,
. ,
irresistible impulse to right action.

In short, while carefully eschewing insane
jealousy of Americans, whom we are bound to
love and respect; senseless Abyssinian expe-
ditions for the benefit of imprudent travellers
who have wandered out of the beaten tracks;
pettifogging Affghan and Persian wars, which,
conductedwith the view of carrying out no great
principle, are therefore wasteful and immoral—
let us cherish instead manly and robust views
of our duty towards our neighbour—France.
Let us, by an unflinching determination to
uphold eternal moral laws, seek to regain that

righieous influence On the Continent whioh
now we have justly forfeited. Let us have a
good large national army for offensive pur.
poses for the same money that is now ex-
pended on numerically' insignificant defen-
sive force, and then, when the time is ripe,
let us peremptorily demand from the Cabinet
of Berlin the immediate restoration of Alsace-
Lorraine on pain of incurring the severe dia.
pleasure of the first military power in EuroPe,
and the most moral State in the world.
JAMES' THOUNTON tOSKINS.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

At a meeting of the Executive Council of the
Agricultural Labourers' Union, held at Leaming-
ton on Monday, it was announced that arrange-
ments were being made for a great mass meeting
of the working men of London in Exeter Hall,
and that Archbishop Manning had expressed him-
self favourably to the Union.
The solicitor of the Union was instructed to
prosecute a farmer at Woodstock who had
assaulted three labourers, and to defend several
ejectmonts for joining the Union. One was
alleged to have occurred in Berkshire, on the
estate of the proprietor of the Times.

Emigration was the subject of a lengthy de-
liberation, and it was resolved to raise a National
Fund to carry it out on a largo scale.
Mr. George Potter, who was present with Mr
Mitchell, asked whether any further information
had been received from the War Office in regard
to the employment of soldiers in harvesting.
Mr. Taylor, the secretary, replied in the
negative.

Gladstone on the subject, and had received the

articles.title: GREAT DEMONSTRATION AT BANBURY.
articles.text:
GREAT DEMONSTRATION AT BANBURY.

Banbury was made a centre of ,the Labourers'
Union on Tuesday under peculiar circumstances.
The Chamber of Agriculture hold its annual
meeting the same day in the same building. The
Chamber met in the Council Chamber, and the
Conference of the Labourers' delegates took place
in the room above, the Town Hall. There was a
largo attendance of delegates, and the district was
formally inaugurated with 2,600 members.
Mr. George Potter, who presided, having opened
the proceedings in an appropriate speech, a com-
mittee and OfileGlS were appointed.
In the afternoon there was a monster tea party
in the Central Corn Exchange. In the evening,
at seven, there was a largo public meeting in the
same place. The chair was occupied by Mr, S. A.
Campbell, J.P., of Rugby, and speeches were de-
livered hy Mr. George Potter, of London, Mr.
George Mitchell, Mr. Arch, and Mr. Henry
Taylor. The speakers showed the advantages of
combination, and resolutions were passed in favour
of the Union. The proceedings throughout were
very enthusiastic.

THE AMALGAMATED TAILORS.

In this month's report tho General Secretary
says

It is once more our privilege and pride to issue
the quarterly report, and record !St ill further ad-

vanees in numlpers, influence, and funds. Since
our last it will be found that branches have been
opened in new districts. Even during the past
season, which is generally one of slackness in our
trade, progress is reported to the extent of 478
members, an increase of funds held by branches of
£704 17s. 3id., and an addition to the permanent

increased by upwards of £1,070 during the

encroachments on the privileges gained during the
past season, and are steadily gaining ground in
material and substantial advantages. We have,
therefore, every reason to hope that, by integrity
in the working and carrying
,into effect of our
rules, we shall so place our society that its bene-
ficial effects may be felt upon the trade for genera-
tions.

To render our society still morn useful and

duty he owes to the trade to constitute himself a
missionary, and assist in spreading its principles
wherever and whenever he may have an oppor-
tunity. Then will be verified the motto on our
escutcheon—" From small beginnings great things
come."

branches.

articles.title: AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF
articles.text:
THE AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF

CARPENTERS.

Mr. Prior in this month's report says:—

A few weeks ago you very wisely decided to
submit the vexed question of the right to use the
Society's name to the decision of five experienced
trades' unionists, selected in consequence of their
known ability and integrity, and their special fit-
ness to thoroughly comprehend and adjudicate on
questions affecting the honour and well-being of
trades' societies.

The selection of these gentlemen was a matter of
mutual agreement, two of them being nominated
by ourselves and three by our opponents.
After eight days spent in carefully analysing
and considering a voluminous mass of evidence
which was laid before them, the arbitrators
unanimously decided that we were entitled to the
sole use of the name of the Amalgamated Society
of Carpenters and Joiners.
This is a great moral triumph. In a court of
law, a just cause is sometimes defeated by some
technical quibble; but the tribunal to which we
have appealed has been guided by the question of
right and wrong, and their decision will be
accepted as binding and final by trades' unionists
and the public generally.
In conferring on us the name of the Society, the
arbitrators have entrusted its honour to our keep-
ing, and it becomes now our duty to guard with
redoubled care against any recurrence of the
jealousy and ill-feeling which has wrought so
much evil in the past.
The arbitrators have recommended a re-union.
This we sincerely desire, and we have offered fair
and equitable terms on which the expelled Branches
may become reinstated in the Society. The mem-
bers of the Gravesend Branch have &ready availed
themselves of this offer, and we have good reasons
for anticipating that many others will speedily
follow their example.

THE SCOTCH ENGINEERS.

On Saturday afternoon, a meeting of the iron
trades of Glasgow and district, convened by the
West of Scotland Iron Trades Short Time League,
was held on Glasgow Green to consider what steps
should be taken with regari to the action of a
largo number of films in connection with the in-
troduction of the 51 hours system, which according
to a mutual agreement come to in February last,
should have taken effect on Friday. It was com-
puted that there were between 11,000 and 13,000
persons present. - -

Mr. Turnbull, chairman of the League, presided,
and stated that a number of the employers had
abandoned the terms resolved upon in the agree-
ment with regard to the Working of the new
system. Not only did they ask an alteration in the
mode of working from what was understood to
have been agreed upon, but they also insisted on a
reduction of the pay.

Mr. Elerick, secretary of the League, intimated
that over twenty firms had already expressed their
willingness to adhere to the terms formerly agreed
upon, but a large number of other firms were still
holding out against the introduction of the terms
of the contract in their entirety. One very large
firm on the Clyde had on Saturday dismissed a
number of men because they would not consent to

WORKMEN'S PEACE ASSOCIATION.

The peaceful settlement of the Alabama dis-
pute, and the second anniversary of the Asso-
ciation, was celebrated on Monday night, at
the Arundel-hall, by a soiree. Several hun-
dreds of the members and friends attended,
the gathering being presided over by Mr.
Edmund Beales, M.A., the hon. president of
the association, who congratulated the meeting
on the settlement of the Alabama dispute, and
on the progress the principle was making.
Mr. Cromer, the secretary, briefly reviewed
the history of the association, which was
publicly inaugurated on September 10, 1870.
He stated that since that time nearly a hun-
dred public meetings, held in different parts of
the country, had endorsed the principles of the
Association, and through its agency nearly
half a million of persons had, by petitions to
the House of Commons, expressed their
for a permanent system of international arbi-
tration. The Association had upwards of a
hundred hon. agents in different towns of the
kingdom engaged in the work of propaganda.
Several communications were made contain-
ing expressions of regret at the inability of
many eminent friends of peace to attend the
gathering, and amongst them was one from the
Hon. Charles Sumner, of the United States
Senate, who, but for the precarious state of his
health, would have been present. Mr. Sumner
expressed his entire approval of the objects of
the meeting, and the principles of the associa-
tion.

Nov.:9, 1872.

MR. RUSKIN ON THE SUNDAY OPEN-

ING OF MUSEUMS.

In this month's number of Fors Clavigera
Mr. John Ruskin has Theseus for his principal
subject of discourse. The statue of that hero,
he remarks, may be seen by working men
whenever they care to see it, though he does
not in the least know why they should care,
and writing to these working men be remarks:
'"•'.4‘ For yearsback, you, or your foolish friends,
have been making a mighty fuss to get your-
selves into the British Museum on Sundays; so
I suppose you want to see the Theseus, or the
. stuffed birds or the crabs and spiders, or the
skeleton of the gorilla, or the parched alliga-
tor skins • and you imagine these contempla-
tions likely to improve and sanctify—that is
to say, recreate your minds. But are you quite
sure you have got any minds yet to be re-
created? Before you expect edification from
that long gallery full of long-legged incon-
ceivable spiders, and colossal blotchy crabs,
did you ever think of looking with any mind
or mindfulness, at the only too easily con-
ceivable short-legged spider of your own Eng-
lish acquaintance? or did you ever so much
as consider why the crabs on Margate sands
were minded to go side-ways instead of
straightforward? Have you so much as
watched a spider making his cobweb, or if you
have not yet had leisure to do that in the toil
of your own cobweb-making, did you ever
think how ho threw his first thread across the
corner P No need for you to go to the British
Museum yet, my friends either on Sundays or
any other slay. 'Well, but the Greek sculpture?
We can't see that at home in our room
corners.' And what is Greek sculpture, or
any sculpture, to you? Are your own legs and
arms not handsome enough for you to look at,
but you must go and stare at chipped and
smashed bits of stones in the likenesses of
legs and arms that ended their walks and
works two thousand years ago? ' Your own
legs and arms are not as handsome as—you
suppose they ought to be,' say you? No; I
fancy not; and you will not make them hand-
somer by sauntering with your hands in your
pockets through the British Museum. Pimp-
pose you will have an agitation, next, for
leave to smoke in it. Go and walk in the
fields on Sunday, making sure, first, therefore,
that you have fields to walk in; look at living
birds not at stuffed ones; and make your own
breasts and shoulders better worth seeing than
the Elgin Marbles." In the course of this
letter Mr. Ruskin makes the confession that
he wrote something when too young and when
he knew only half truths, and was eager to set
them forth by what he thought fine words.
"People," he says, "used to call me a good
writer then; now they say I can't write at
all; because, for instance, if I think any.
body's house is on fire, I only say, 'Sir, your
house is on fire;' whereas formerly I used to
say, Sir, the abode in which you probably
passed the delightful days of youth is in a state
of inflammation,' and everybody used to like
the effect of the two p's in 'probably passed,'
and of the two d's in ' delightful days. "

articles.text:
STATISTICS OF RELIGIOUS ACCOMMO-

DATION.

The Nonconformist of Wednesday pub-
lishes a second supplement, in continuance of
the one issued a fortnight since. That supple-
ment gave the statistics of religious accom-
modation in the fourteen large towns of more
than 100,000 inhabitants; Wednesday's sup-
plement contains similar statistics of the pro,.
vision made by the various denominations in
twenty towns which have more than 50,000
and less than 100,000 inhabitants.
The towns dealt with in the present returns
are as follows:—
Bath, Halifax, Preston,
Birkenhead, Leicester, Rochdale,
Blackburn, Merthyr Southampton,
Bolton Norwich,, Stockport,
(Judd, Nottingham, Sunderland,
Derby, Oldham Swansea,
Davenport, Plymouth.
The aggregate population in these towns were
in 1851, 966,124; in 1872, it is 1,439,816;
an increase of 473,692. The number of places
of worship in them in 1851 was, according to
the Census, 745, with 423,600 sittings; in
1872 there are I,OCI places of worship, with
666,443 sittings; an increase of 256 buildings
and 242,843 sittings. The growth of religious
accommodation in those towns is therefore
selatively larger than in the fourteen great
towns. In the great towns the population has
Increased 42.4 per cent., and the provision for
religious worship 44 per cent; in these towns
of second rank the growth of the population
has been 49.3 per cent., while the increase of
accommodation in places of warship has been
67.3 per cent.; so that in twenty years of
purely voluntary effort the increased provi-
sion for religious worship has gained on the
increase of the population, so as considerably
to reduce the defielency which the religious
Census of 1851 disclosed.

The relative proportions of the Established
Church and of the unestablished Churches are
as follows :—Of the 1,001 places of worship
and the 666,443 sittings, the Established
Church owns 292 of the buildings and
322,878 of the sods; the nva-e§tablighea

Churches provide 809 of the places and
443,565 of the sittings. The Census of 1851
gave the places of worship as 214 and 531 re-
spectively, and the sittings as 162,457 and
261,143. Assuming these figures to have
been correct, the Established Church had in
that year 38.3 per cent. of the sittings, whereas
it now has 33.4 per cent.; the other Churches
had 61.7, and now have 66.6. The Estab-
lished Church is therefore so far in a relatively
worse position than it was twenty-one years
ago.

articles.title: AMNESTY DEMONSTRATION IN HYDE PARK.
articles.text:
THE AMNESTY DEMONSTRATION IN
HYDE PARK.

The appeal made to the working classes by
the Fenian Amnesty Committee brought
together on Sunday last in Hyde Park a large
assemblage. The crowd gathered in that
portion of the park where the Commissioner of
Works bad placed the stone and iron pillars
to denote the spot where public addresses
might be delivered.
At half-past three o'clock, Mr. J. Chaddock,
was voted to the chair, and the business of the
meeting at once commenced.
Mr. Bailey moved the first resolution, as
follows :

Resolved, that the first and dearest right of man
is the right to resist injustice and oppression, and
those men who in whatever age or nation have
been foremost in resisting tyranny arc among the
great benefactors of the human race, have won
from history its highest tribute of appluase, and
made examples which will at all risks be imitated
among men for all time to come; and that political
prisoners are men of this type, who bravely stepped
forward from the ranks of their countrymen to
protest against and resist, at the peril of their lives,
the most galling system of oppression known
among the civilized nations of the present day;
that Mr. Gladstone, the Prime Minister, was the
foremost man in England four years ago to justify
the Fenians and accept office upon the avowed
platform of redressing the grievances which drove
them to revolt, and it appears to this meeting a
saddening inconsistency on his part to hold those
patriots in dungeons in opposition to the oft-
declared sentiments of millions of people in
Ireland and elsewhere, and in conflict with the
public opinion which raised him to power as an
Englishman and a friend of humanity.
Mr. Mooney seconded the resolution.
The resolution was carried unanimously,
followed by loud cheering.

Mr. C. Murray moved the second. resolu-
tion :

Resolved, that this meeting expresses its un-
bounded abhorrence of the practice of degrading
political prisoners to the class of felons, enforcing
upon them the horrors of the silent system, and
otherwise subjecting them to a cruel and vindic-
tive rdgitne, repugnant to ovary human instinct,
and disgraceful to our vaunted civilisation; that
the said treatment of Fenian prisoners considered
in conjunction with the Algerme•like rule of the
Government in Ireland and the treatment of the
so•called " rebels " in Jamaica and India, com-
bines to exhibit the true spirit of British policy,
and contrasts most strikingly
,and unfavourably
with that of the United States of America after
the suppression of a protracted and sanguinary
civil war; this meeting, therefore, demands the
immediate and unconditional release of all the
said prisoners, as also the repeal of the parlia-
mentary enactments by which such odious treat-
ment is sanctioned.

Mr. P. O'Leary seconded the resolution,
which was supported by Mr. Funnel!, and
carried unanimously.
Mr. Canham moved the third and last re-
solution, which was as follows :
Resolved, that, should our demands be not
conceded, this meeting pledges itself to form an
Amnesty Association for the purpose of promoting
and holding meetings throughout Great Britain in
conjunction with the Irish Amnesty Association,
and continuo active operations until the whole of
the Fenian prisoners, civil and military, shall be
sot at liberty; and, moreover, we call upon the
working men of England to oppose any candidate
for Parliament who shall refuse to pledge himself
to release these ill-treated men, and also to repeal
the unconstitutional laws that now prevail in Ire -
land, which grievously afflict the :unfortunate
people of that misgoverned country.
Mr. De Morgan seconded the resolution,
which was supported by Mr. M'Donnell and
Mr. Pottle, and agreed to.
The united bodies left the Park in procession
at five o'clock, in good order, singing " God
save Ireland."

Superintendent Williamson, of Scotland-
yard, accompanied by a gentleman from the
Board of Works, applied to Mr. Mewton, at the
Marlborough-street police-court on Monday,
for summonses against the speakers at the
Fenian meeting in Hyde-park, on Sunday, for
acting in contravention of the Park Regulation
Act. Mr. Newton said he saw by the papers
that morning that the Act of Parliament was
not a valid Act; therefore the addresses de-
livered by the speakers were lawful addresses.
He should like to have the matter properly
argued, before granting the application. The
Superintendent asked if the magistrate would
like that to be done before granting the sum-
monses? Mr. Newton said in that case no one
would be before him. Whether it was an Act
of Parliament or not the magistrates were being
tl.a.ced in a somewhat ludicrous position. Mr.
aox, had informed him that according to the

Law Officers of the Crown the Act was a valid
Act, but in the papers of that morning the
contrary was stated. The Gentleman from
the Board of Works said he might state that
the opinion of the Law Officers of the Crown
was taken on Saturday, and they were clearly
of opinion that the Act could be enforced. Mr.
Newton said the magistrates at that court had,
under the Act, been asked to send poor persons
to prison for selling pictures, medals, and such
things in the Park, and yet a fair had been
permitted by the police to take place in the
Park on Sunday, without interference. He
should order the summonses to issue.

THE EAST AFRICA.N SLATE TRADE.

A crowded and enthusiastic meeting, pre-
sided over by the Lord Mayor, was held on
Monday at the Mansion-house, to pass reso-
lutions on the evils of the existing African
slave trade. Large numbers of ladies and
gentlemen were unable to obtain admission,
and the speakers, owing to the thronged pas-
sages, with difficulty made their way to the
platform. Amongst the distinguished persons
present were the Baroness Burdett-Coutts, tho
Rev. It. Moffatt (the veteran South African
missionary), Mr. IL M. Stanley, the Hon. A.
Kinnaird, Bishops Claughton and Ryan, Mr.
Otway, M.P., Mr. Gilpin, M.P., Lord Law-
rence, &o. Mr. Stanley, who was received
with much cheering, sat to the Lord Mayor's
left, and the Bishop of Winchester to his
right.
kAfter a few pertinent and appropriate re-
marks from the Lord. Mayor, the Bishop of
Winchester moved the first resolution, viz. :
That the same imperative duty which rested on
Great Britain to suppress the West African slave
trade, binds her to the suppression of that from
the east coast.

The rev. gentleman eloquently exposed the
cruelties perpetrated by the East African
slave-traders, who make the country explored
by Livingstone the basis of their operations,
and urged the necessity of England putting a
little friendly pressure on the :Sultan of
Zanzibar. _ _ _ .

The motion was seconded by Mr. Kirkman
Hodgson, M.P., and carried.
Mr. Stanley, who was next called upon by
the Lord Mayor, was received with loud and
long cheering. At first it was insisted by the
outer wing of the audience that ho should
stand upon a chair, and he did so, but after
explaining that he should be unable to speak
from such a platform, ho descended amidst
laughter and renewed applause, upon a level
with the rest of the speakers. He said he had
been requested to move the second resolution—

That all who desire to promote the abolition of
this trade should make its enormities as widely
known as possible.

It was for this purpose he was present. The
enormities of the slave trade Livingstone took
as his text letter after letter. "Why P The
litany of the slave trade had not resounded in
the ears of Christian nations as it had re-
sounded in that ball. David Livingstone had
brought the theme before us. He had sung
their complaints over and over again. At the
time he was supposed to have been lost in a
dark and fabulous region, he commissioned
him (Mr. Stanley) to carry the complaints to
England. He had done so,. and had now to
tell the meeting what he had seen personally
as regarded the slave trade. Ho • would not
attempt any grand sensationalistic pictures,
for fear he might be dubbed with that adjec-
tive which a gentleman and a kind Christian
endowed him with at Brighton. After a for-
cible and telling speech, in which Mr. Stanley
said he was convinced that the suavity of Sir
Bartle Freres eminently fitted him for the deli-
cate and difficult duty he would have to dis-
charge, and also that he was clearly of opinion
that the British Foreign Minister need not
hesitate to use very decisive measures to sup-
press the nefarious traffic, the resolution was
seconded and carried unanimously.
Sir Bartle Frere spoke of the desirability of
the political measures of the Government hav-
ing the co-operation of commercial men.
Bishop Claughton, Bishop Ryan, Lord Har-
rowby, Lord Lawrence, Mr. Otway, M.P., the
Rev. Dr. Moffatt, Mr. Kirkman Hodgson,
M.P., also spoke, and other resolutions were
adopted in sympathy with the object of the
meeting, pledging themselves to petition Par-
liament against the enormities existing in the
African slave trade.

After the usual vote of thanlcs, the proceed-
ings terminated.

acres of land under water. ,

The granting of privileged HOOllOOB to
public...houses in the neighbourhood of the
metropolitan theatres formed the subject of' a
deputation to Colonel llenderson on Monday.
The Commissioner confessed that the issue of
these privileges was a most invidious duly,
and one surrounded with dilllenity.Ha
suggested that if the theatres were to close
-
somewhat earlier there would be no occasion
for any extension of time to any public-house
whatever; and be expressed his belief that by
this means the views of all concerned would
be met.

The dinner in celebration of the opening of
telegi'apliie communication with Australia is
fixed for Friday, the 15th inst., at the earnloll-
- Hotel. The Earl of Kimberley will
take the chair, and will be supported by a
number of noblemen and o'entlemen iutorested
in the colonie;>.
