IB WBEKI3 NZWS.

The Prince of Wales, through his private
secretary, has expressed his earnest hope that
Sheffield will be represented at the Vienna
)rlaibition, and says he will be greatly in-
debted to Mr. Mandella, M.P. if that gentle-
man will draw attention to the subject.

The Duke of Edinburgh has been strongly
pressed to become an admiral, but he firmly
declines to take a flag until he has had some
experience as captain in an iron-clad ship, and
the Sultan is designated as the vessel lie is
desirous to command.

An event which has been regarded as of
great consequence to the future of China, both
in respect to her domestic concerns and to her
foreign relations, took place at Pekin on the
16th of last month, when the Emperor was
married. Beyond the procession of the bride
to the Palace there was no public ceiemony,
ana everything passed off quietly.

The Governor of the Cape Colony has visited
the Diamond Fields, and been well received.
He delighted the diggers with a promise to
recommend the erection of West Griqualand
into a separate Crown colony.

The list of cases in the Divorce Court has
been issued. The total is 261, of which
thirteen are standing over by consent. Of the
248 to be beard 187 are to be without juries.

Madame Patti has made her debut at Mos-
cow in the " Traviata " with tremendous
success, having been recalled during the re-
presentation thirty times. The boaquet of
camelias thrown by the Princess Dolgorouki
Was so large as to require two men to carry it
across the stage, and the value of the Rowers
showered upon the famous eautatrice amounted
to £lOO.

The Agricultural Labourers' Union have
commenced sending out labourers and their
families to Queensland from Minster, Isle of
Thomet.

The opening of the Law Courts on Satur-
day, when the new Lord Chancellor and Mr.
Sustice Denman made their first appearances
on the benoh, was marked with an exceptional
amount of public interest. Both Lord Se-
borne and the new Pullin° Judge received a
very gratifying ovation. In receiving the now
Lord Mayor (Sir Sydney Waterlow), the Lord
Chancellor paid a graceful tribute to the
public spirit of the Corporation.

At a meeting held at Rouen of the commer-
cial community for tho relief of the Alsatian
and Lorraine emigrants, M. Pouyer-Quertier
appealed for subscriptions, and said that more
than 200,000 of these emigrants were in the
frontier towns. The late Minister of Finance
said that ho had seen the mayors of the
occupied towns, and they all told him they
dreaded the opening of the Fronoh papers,
fearing that the attacks on the Prussians would
lead them to make reprisals on the inhabi-
tants.

An extraordinary robbery has been joerpo-
trated at Carlisle. A boy in the Caledonian
Railway office was sent with a day's receipts,
amounting to £125, for the purpose of bank-
ing the money. On his way he had a fit, and
when he was found some time later the whole
of the money had boon carried off. The boy is
subject to fits.

For the present term there are forty cases to
be heard in the Probate Court, of which
twenty are without juries.

It is said that a sister of Mr. Spurgeon is
preaohing with much success at Willingham,
in Cambridgeshire, where her husband is a
Baptist minister. The eases from Willing-
ham tried before the local bench have de-
creased to such an extent that the police
authorities have expressed their thanks to the
lady preacher as being the instrument of the
improvement.

Mr, Bancroft, the 'United States Minister at
Berlin, having offered to repay the expenses
incurred in the San Juan arbitration, has been
thanked by the Prussian Minister for Foreign
Affairs, and informea that there are none.

The horse epidemic, which has committed
such ravages in America, has made its appear-
slice in several parts of Devonshire. In the
neighbourhood of Tiverton it has assumed
Considerable proportions.

It is stated that the death of Dr. Go!s, the
Roman Catholic Bishop of Liverpool, Will sfl-
able certain alterations to be carried into
effect which have for some d i
dine been n con-
templation by the Roman Catholic hierarchy,
and that a new bishopric—that of Lancaster—
will and that the diocese of Liver-
pool will be made into an arch-diocese, in-.
eluding Lancaster, Salford, Beverley, and
probably another of the larger towns of the
north,

The new Treaty of Commerce with Frtune
was again under discussion by the Manchester
Chamber of Commerce on Monday; and, al-
though no formal resolution was come to,
there appears to have been a general agree-
ment with the chairman (Mr; fitugh Mason),
Mr. Jacob Bright; and Sir E. Viratkin, that it
would be better to be without a Treaty at all
than to make any fresh sacriace of the priaci-
pies of Free Trade.

Mr. Darwin has produced, in support of his
theory of evolution, and in necessary corro-
boration of his "Descent of Man," his eagerly
expected work on the expression of the emo-
tions in man and animals. The work is an
elaborate defence of the theory,. in opposition
to Sir Charles Bell's celebrated essay, that the
habit of expressing our feelings by certain
muscular movements, though now rendered
innate, had been in some manner acquired;
or, in other words, that the nervous and 'Ma-
cular specialization by which particular emo-
tions are indicated is the result of habit, in-
herited peculiarity, and natural development
—the principle of selection, as exhibited in
the individual.

A military deputation from St. 'Petersburg
is at present in Berlin, charged with the
presentation to Prince Charles of the Order of
St. George, and bearing a letter from the Czar
congratulating the Prince on the 60th anniver-
sary of his appointment to the coloneloy of the
6th Russian Musketeer Regiment, represented
by the deputation. Emphasis is given to this
ceremonial by the expression of the Czar's
desire in the autograph epistle "to draw
closer the ties which unite us," and the hope
that the friendship thus signalised may endure
for future generations.

On Monday the Prince and Princess of Wales
visited the Maharajah Dhuleep Singh, at his
residence at Thetford, in Norfolk, and met
with an enthusiastic reception.

Tiverton election resulted in the _return,
after an exciting struggle, of Mr. Massey, the
Liberal candidate. The intense interest that
was felt in the contest is shown by the fact
that in a constituency numbering little over
1,200, no fewer than 1,124 electors went to the
poll. At the dose the figures were—Massey, 577;
Walrond, 547. The Conservatives had to
suffer a double defeat; for during the day,
relying upon the Preston expedient, they had
confidently anticipated the opening of the
ballot, box, and proclaimed themselves
victorious.

In the Court of Common Pleas Miss Alice
Tournay brought an action for breach of
promise of marriage against a young farmer,
named Kingsnorth, who (toted as his father's
bailiff, and who had broken his word to the
plaintiff on the discovery ho made, after the
purchase of the wedding•ring, that he had. not
the means to marry. A letter which ho had
written to " My dearest Alice," and in which
the writer amusingly detailed the incon-
veniences of a baohelor's life, was read in
court. Damages to the extent of £2OO was
given against the inconstant suitor.

At Marylebone, Mr. Horace Grey was fined
20s. and °oats for attempting to enter a train
while in motion at Hampstead-heath Station.

On Monday the barque Suzerain, of Scar-
borough, put into Sorabster, having been in
collision with the Liverpool ship Oceanian, of
8,946 tons, during a gale fifty miles north of
Cape Wrath. During the hurry and confusion
of the collision the crew of the Suzerain
attempted to scramble on board the larger
vessel; and the captain and carpenter fell
down between the ships and were drowned. It
was soon found that the Oceanioa was sinking,
and a rush was made for the barque. Nine-
teen of the Oceanica's crew were unable to
reach her, and had barely got into their boat
when their vessel sank. They remained with-
out rood or water from Wednesday till Friday,
when the weather .moderated sufficiently to
to allow of their -being taken on board the
Suzerain, which was with difficulty kept afloat
till she reached Scrabster.

The selection of Air. Baron Cleasby as the
Court of Exchequer election judge, during the
ensuing year, has already been announced.
The 'choice of the other courts has now been
made, Mr. Justice Blackburn having been
selected from the Queen's Bench, and
_Mr.
Justice Keating from the Common Pleas.

During the week ending Saturday last 5,363
births and 3,163 deaths were registered in
London and twenty other large cities and
towns of the United kingdom. The mortality
from all clauses in these towns was at a rate of
22 deaths annually to every 1,000 persons
estimated to be living. In the metropolis
2,291 births and 1,306 deaths were registered,
the former having been 34, and the latter 230
below the average. 14 persons died from
small-pc; 12 from measles, 21 from scarlet
fever, 2 from diphtheria, 28 from whooping-
cough, 24 from different forms of foyer, and
18 from diarrlicea,

The first municipal election under the ballot
took place in the Scotch burghs on Taesday.
In Edinburgh the proceedings were charac-
terised by unusual order and quiet, though
there was a contest in ten out .of the thirty
wards, and the ballot was found to work ad-
mirably, The card system was adopted for
the purpose of ascertaining the results of the
toting, but generally without success;

Mr. Pales, QC., the new Attorney-General
for Ireland, addressed a large meeting of the
electors at Londonderry on Tuesday. Before
the time of meeting a number of the lower
orders got possession of the building, a large
factory, and attempted to prevent Mr. Palies
being heard by Home Rule cries and interrup-
tions. Mr. Palles, however succeeded in
making,himself heard, and delivered a power-
ful speech, vindicating the measures of the
Administration. The meeting broke up in
disorder.

An engineer named Burt, belonging to the
Asia, pleaded guilty, at a court-martial held
at Portsmouth on Tuesday, to the charge of
drunkenness, and having been previously tried
by court-martial, was sentenced to be dis-
missed the service. A second-class stoker,
named Edward Ryan, for using threatening
language, and striking the leading stoker, was
ordered to be imprisoned for two years, and
dismissed the service.

A special telegram from a Correspondent at
Rheims reports the evacuation of that town by
the Germans, whose place will be taken by the
French troops as soon a'4 the barracks, which
are reported to be in an unsanitary state, are
ready to receive them. The officer charged
with an indiscreet Imperialist speeoh at La
Fere has been sent on a mission to Algeria.

Lewes kept up in 1872 the annual saturnalia
by which it commemorates the event of Nor. 6,
1605. Fireworks, bonfires, and torchlight
processions helped to make the display, which,
happily, no other place attempted to rival.
Generally the day passed very quietly.

-Mr. Frank Buckland announces the birth of
a young hippopotamus, which took place at
the Zoological Gardens on Tuesday morning.
The little stranger is about three and a half feet
long, and weighs nearly a hundredweight; and
the greatest precautions are taken to save it
from the too early fate of all its species hither-
to born in Europe. If it survive it will be
called Guy Fawkes."

Lord Westbury decided, in the European
Assurance Arbitration, the case of Mr. Wall-
berg, laying down the principles, that the time
at which the valuation of policies and annui-
ties should be made was not the date of the
presentation of the petition for winding-up,
but the date of the winding-up order; and
that policy holders who had received back
premiums from the " suspense account," must
repay them to the official liquidator before they
could prove. The learned Lord does not sit
again until January.

At the Middlesex Sessions, Agnes Aravon,
Frenchwoman, was convicted of obtaining
550 f. from Annette •Ditsoir by falsely pre-
tending to possess influence which she was to
use in Madlle. Dusoir's favour with the Em-
peror Napoleon. An old lady who had trusted
the prisoner had been even more artlessly
victimised. She was condemned to twelve
months' hard labour.

On Tuesday the Archbishop of Canterbury,
in receiving a number of clergy at Tunbridge,
spoke of the relation in which the Church of
England stood to other religious bodies, both
at home and abroad. Although many had
adversely criticized the convening of the Pan-
Anglican Synod of 1867 by Archbishop Long-
ley, he believed that the course then taken was
a.wise one, and likely to engender a spirit of
brotherly feeling amongst the Churches repre-
sented at that gathering. And while it was
important to hold out the right hand of fellow-
ship to their foreign brethren, it should be
remembered that there were many to whom
they wore strangers at home, and every effort
ought to be made to draw them into the bends
of fellowship and love.

The opening of the City Library and Museum
was celebrated at Guildhall on Tuesday even-
ing, when a numerous and brilliant gathering
assembled to meet Lord Chancellor Selborne
on this his first official visit to the City of
London since his elevation to the Woolsack.

The Rev. Dr. Cookson, master of St. Peter's
College, has been elected Vice-Chancellor of
the University of Cambridge.

it is stated that Mr. Andrew Rutherford
Clark, the Solicitor -General for Scotland, will
be a candidate for the representation of Orkney
and Shetland in opposition to Mr. Laing, Just
now the Government is short of its proper
legal strength in Parliament, for besides the
Scottish Solioitor-General, neither of the Irish
Law offloors has a seat in the House of Com-
mons.

It is stded by the Taris Libert..e that
smuggling has greatly increased in the north
of France, and that the Government is taking
measures against it.

An American seaman named. Crank has been
charged at Bow-street with the wilful mut.. der
of John Rodgers, a fellow-sailor, upon the
high seas, and also with assaulting the asptaia
of the ship (the Top Gallant) with intent' to
murder him. The evidence did not support
either of the charges, and as the Offence .nf
m anslaughter is net included in the Extradition
Treaty with the United States, and as the
first-mentioned charge amounted to that only,
Sir Thomas Henry decided that be .could not
surrender the prisoner to the American Govern-
ment. He will therefore be discharged.

Mr. Arnold, tho Westminster police raagis -
trate, in the course •Of some School Board
prosecutions which came before him expressed
his opinion that the law was defective in
having made no provision for examining the
defendants on oath. Although the power to do
so was not given under the Education Act it
existed under the Factory. Act. .

During the election at Tiverton on Monday,
just after nine o'clock, a pensioner, named
Hawkins, was assisted to one of the booths
for the purpose of voting for Walrond, and
while the customary questions were being put
to him, he became unconscious from excite-
ment. On being carried out he died almost
immediately, his decease being attributed to
heart disease.

At the Petty Sessions, King's- heath, near
Birmingham, Mr. James Crump, a farmer,
was fined 40s. and costs, under the Adultera-
tion Act, for selling milk which contained 25
per cent. of water, without declaring it to be
a mixture at the time of sale.

The Metropolitan Free Bridges' Association
has resolved to strengthen, in every possible
way, the hands of the Board of Works in the
effort which is to be made to throw open
thok bridges over the Thames upon which a
toll is at present charged.

M. Grevy, it is stated, has expressed to g.
Thiers a strong disinclination to accept the
Vice-Presidenoy of the Republic on the ground
that it would appear fo give thin rtndue
finence in presiding layer the debates in tho
Assembly.

A fresh conflict between Church and Stato
has arisen in Switzerland. Some time ago ,a
Jesuit Father, named Allet, was appointed
.our 6 of Loueche, in the Valais. According to
the Swiss Constitution, however, the members
of the Order of the Jesuits are forbidden to
exercise any functions either in the sehoOls or
the churches. The Federal Council has
accordingly requested the State Connell of
Valais to refuse its ratification to the appoint-
ment. The appointment is meanwhile defended
by the Bishop in whose diocese Loueche is
situated, who maintains that 1.1. Allot has been
admitted among the clergy of that diooosef
and is now under episeopal jurisdiction.

A gentleman has been killed at Teignmouth
by falling from a cliff 255 ft. high. The de-
ceased was a wharfinger in London named
Toole.

Samuel Gee, pedestrain, of Willenhall, was
lined 40A. and costs at the Tipton Police-court
on Monday, for an assault on the Venerabl9
Archdeacon Moore, at Wecln.esburylwat
Station on Saturday night.

A correspondent in Italy, writing kali
Ferrara on the 30th ult., gives a melancholy
picture of the inundated districts. Trees lip
fiat on the ground, rooted up by the force of
the goods. The meadows and fields arestrewn,
with sand and stones. One.third of thelionseo
facing the river at Cassalmaggiore are en!!
tirely covered by the water. Those which tiro
not destroyed are abandoned. The wealthy
have fled the neighbourhood ; the poor wander
about, trusting to charity for their subsii-
tepee. No such inundation of the Po has
been seen during the present century.

During the seven months from April 1 to
November 2 the Exchequer receipts amounted
to £40,138,187, as compared with 37,582,918
in the corresponding period of last year. The
expenditure has been £43,3M,777. On Satur-
day last the balance in the Bank of Engl.and
was rather more than three millions sterling.

A numerously-attended council meeting of
the Central Chamber of Agriculture vras held.
on Tuesday at the Salisbury Hotel. The re-
port of the Local Taxation Committee alluded
at considerable length to the results of the
efforts made by Sir Massey Lopes and others
to keep this question before the attention of
the public; and, with respect to the probable
proposals of the Government next session, it
was stated that County financial Boards; as an
administrative reform, would have the cordiat
support of the Committee. 7

Admiral Sir Sydney Daores has accepted the
post of Visitor and Governor of Greenwich
Hospital. No decision, we believe, has yet
been made as to Sir Sydney's successor in the
office of Lord Commissioner, but Admiral Sir
Alexander Milne and Vice-Admiral Sir
Hastings Yelverton have both been named in
connection with the honour.

On account of the dissatisfaction caused by
the permission given to six publicans at
Brighton to keep open one hour longer than
the rest—three of the houses being near the
theatre—the privilege has been revoked.

For the vacancy caused by Mr. Maguire's
death the most probable candidate at present
is Mr. Mathew, a relative of Father Mathew,
the celebrated "apostle" of temperance. Mr.
Ronayne declines to come forward, and Mr.
Shaw will not relinquish his seat for Bandon.
The Nationalist party cannot support a candi-
date with any prospect of success.

Prince Arthur returned to Dover from
Windsor Castle, where his B,oyal Highness
went on Friday, on Monday morning, and
resumed duty with his regiment.

A verdict of temporary insanity has been
returned in the one of a man at Donnybrook,
who, after inflicting serious injuries on a little
girl with a razor, cut his own throat.

Mr. Horner, secretary to the Wolverhampton
Gas Company, has absconded. He was en-
gaged with some of the directors at the offices
of the company on Friday, and remained there
until a late hour. On Saturday he was
Missing. An examination showed that he had
taken with him all the cash that was in the
office on Friday night, amounting to a good
sum, and there is also a deficieney in his
accounts.

Two hundred and eighty-five patients were
relieved at the British Hospital for Diseases of
the Skin, Finsbury-square, and Great Marl-
borough-street, during the week ending Nov.
2nd.

In the Church Synod on Monday the ruling
of Judge Harrison, to the effect that a motion
on the subject of the ritual was ultra vireo led
to excited debate, and an effort was made to
prevent the signing of the minutes. It is
intended to raise the question in another form,
whether the Synod is to be confined to the
temporalities of the Church.

At a meeting of the Agricultural Labourers'
Union held at Leamington on Monday, it was
stateethat A.rohbishop Manning has expressed
verbally to the secretary his warm sympathy
with the labourers' movement and his desire
to see their condition improved.

On the 7th of October, Albert Thaokeray,
aged 10, son of the lleadingly Church school-
master at Leeds, was patting a large dog, when
the animal bit him on the forehead and cheek.
The boy showed no symptoms of illness until
the 27th, and on that day he was returning
home from Sunday-school when a dog barked
and ran towards him. Immediately he exhi-
bited signs of illness. Arrived at home, he
complained of headaohe, chilliness, Jo., and
gradually became worse, exhibiting all the
symptoms of hydrophobia until Thursday,
when he died. An inquest was held on Mon-
day, and the dog was ordered to be destroyed.
Only on Monday last, the Leicester School
Board, which has been in existence nearly two
years, appointed a committee for the purpose
of framing bye-laws. No schools have yet been
erected by the board, kit provision for 6,000
children is contemplated,

The large drapery warehouse of Messrs.
Nathaniel Evans and Co. of Limerick, was
burned to the ground early on Mondayinorning.
The entire street was endangered.

liir. Mitchel, formerly M.P. for Bodmin,
died at Plymouth on, Monday morning.

A woman, named Ann Waring, has died at
Leyland who had for some time been receiving
parochial relief. After her death it was fouud
that she was possessed of 4300.

The Blackpool Looal Board have resolved
upon the erection of a new market, which is
to be erected in West-street and Lytham-
street.

The corner stone of a new Masonic) hall for
Liverpool, in Hope-street, has been laid with
full Slanonie honours by Brother the Right
Hon. Lord Skeltnersdale. In the evening a
grand banquet was given at the Adelphi Hotel;
Lord Skeltnersdale presiding.

A Berlin telegram iii the Globe states that
the Prussian Government, in consequence of
the alarming progress of cholera, has invited
physicians and surgeons to place themselves
lit Oa service of the Government, offering
them a remuneration of five dialers per clay,
besides travelling expenses and free use of
carriages and horses,

The funeral of Mr. Maguire, M.P., which
took place in the Mathew Cemetery, Cork, on
Tuesday, gave rise to the most imposing de-
monstration ever witnessed in that city. All
the shops were closed, and business was
entirely suspended. The Mayor and Corpora-
tion, the Harbour Commissioners, and other
public bodies, the Trades Associations to the
number of seven or eight thousand, drapers'
assistants, the constabulary wearing side arms,
the charitable associations and children of
the sohools, and a great concourse of mourners
from every: town in the southern counties,
appeared in the procession. The pall Was
borne by eight gentlemen, including Mr.
Downing, M.P., Mr. Murphy, the High
Sheriff, dm

Mr. H. n Stanley delivered a lecture in St.
jaMOS'I3 Hall, on Tuesday evening last, on his
adventures in Central Africa, and his remi-
niscences of Dr. Livingstone. The hall was
filled, and Mr. Stanley was very warmly re-
ceived.

Mr. Kinnaird, M.P., presided on Tuesday at
a meeting of the Golden-lane Mission, at which
it was announced that new premises, the site
of which has not yet been selected, are to be
erected for its use.

A deputation from Marylebone, headed by
Mr. Harvey Lewis, M.P., had an interview
with Col. Henderson on the subject of the
exemptions under the Licensing Act, of which
the deputation complained. In reply, the
Commissioner stated that this was the only
practical difficulty that had arisen in the work-
ing of the enactment, and ho thought it might
be surmounted if the theatres would close a
little earlier. He vindicated the exemptions
as clearly intended by the Legislature and as
being strictly limited to the requirements of
the public; and fluidly promised to submit
the question raised to th Home Secretary.

At Ashton-under-Lyne a torchlight pro-
cession of about 10,000 people took place on
Sunday *night, and at one time seriously
threatened the peace of the town, in con-
sequence of the closing of the public-houses at
nine o'clock. At Hull, where also the nine
o'clock closing came into operation, the public
peace was threatened by a large mob which
assembled in the Market-place.

Paul julius Mai, the survivor of that which
has been known as the Chelsea tragedy, was
brought up at the Westminster Police-court,
on Monday, charged with the wilful murder of
Hermann Nagle. Mr. Poland appeared for
the prosecution on behalf of the Crown. Evi-
dence of identity only was taken, and the pri-
soner, who urged that he was still very unwell,
was committed to the Old Bailey for trial.

A well-dressed, powerful young man was
on Monday convicted at the Thames Police-
court of an outrageous assault on a respectable
married woman at a late hour on Saturday
night. He pleaded drunkenness as a pallia-
tion of the offanoe, but the magistrate sent
him to prison for two mouths, with hard
labour.

A very large number of defendants on Mon-
day answered at the police-courts to charges
of drunkenness. At Lambeth alone there were
twenty-seven such, besides eleven other
offenoes under the new Act, and at Worship-
street thirty-three.

The Rev. C. J. Bird, Vicar of Christchurch,
West Fordington, Dorchester. has resigned his
living on aceount of the Bennett judgment.
He preached his farewell sermon on Sunday
night.

On Monday evening the Farmers' Club held
their first meeting after the autumnal recess,
and there was a full attendance. The ques-
tion of seourity of tenure was introduced by
Mr. T. Honey, of Warwickshire, and it was
diecussed at great length. The feeling was
strongly in favour of compensation being
allowed for unexhausted improvements.

An alarming fire occurred on Monday in
Duneeht House, twelve miles from Aberdeen,
which belongs to the Earl of Crawford and
Balcarres, and is occupied by his eldest son,
Lord Lindsay. With the help of fire-engines
from Aberdeen, it was confined to the wing
where the servants sleep, which was almost
entirely destroyed. While the fire was at its
height, the inarticulate cries of a deaf and
dumb lady's maid were heard issuing from
one of the rooms where the fire was raging,
and Lord Lindsay heroically darted through
the flames,
and brought her safely to the out-
side a few seconds before the roof fell with a
great crash.

The Tweed and the White Adder are flooded
by the ht,avy rains. Considerable damage
has been done near Berwick by inundations
and landslips.

The foot-and-mouth disease, recently very
prevalent throughout Warwiokshire, bas nearly
disappeared.

A riot is reported from a coal mulling
district in the department of Gird, Ftanoe. A
band of 150 men having attacked an ootroi
station, and wounded several gendarmes, the
latter used their firearms. Two of the rioters
were killed and one wounded. '

The danger of inundation which threatened
Mantua seems to be averted. A large number
of small steamers and boats had come from
Venice to render assistance, and trains,- laden
with bread and other food, were arriving from
all parts. Victor Emmanuel has subscribed
40,000 francs, and. the Pope 6,000 francs, in
aid of the sufferers of the inundations.

The first of the eleventh series of Lambeth
Baths Winter Meetings has been inaugurated
by a meeting under the chairmanship of Mr.
Samuel Morley, M.P. In the course of the
evening the hon. gentleman distributed the

SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 9, 1872.

THE INEVITABLE QUESTION IN
PRUSSIA.

THE :problem of second Chambers in Con-
stitutional States once more presses for solu-
tion. The Landlords' House in Prussia has
by an overwhelming majority thrown out a
measure of so-called Reform which had the
approbation of the Crown and of tho repre-
sentatives of the people. Of unavoidable
consequence, the citizens and the journalists of
the capital are eagerly discussing with each
other the necessity of dealing with the refrac-
tory branch of the Legislature, and the im-
perative expediency of different modes of
meeting the emergency. The advanced section
of the Liberal party in the elective Chamber
avow the intention to make the reconstruction
of the other chamber a principal question at
the next elections. Prussia is too imperfectly
a Constitutional State, in our broad sense of
the expression, for the EMPEROR-KING to
reserve altogether his own opinion and feeling
on the occasion; but there is nothing offen-
sively monarchical in the declaration attributed
to his MAJESTY, that the House which has
thrown out a measure, having the sanction of
the other two estates of the realm, must by
some means be brought into harmony with the
legislative necessities of the time. By present
arrangement, a place for repentance is pro-
vided. The rejection of the ministerial mea-
sure was immediately followed by a proroga-
tion of Parliament; but the Chambers will
meet for a new session on the twelfth instant.
The same or a similar Bill will then be sub-
mitted. If that should pass both Houses,
well; but, if, while accepted by the Deputies,
it shall be refused by the aristocrats, no other
course will remain open but some such recon-
struction of the obstructive Chamber as may
meet in a more practicable spirit the supposed
demands of general opinion,

The rejected measure is styled a Counties
Reform Bill. The subject matter has been in
agitation, more or less, for many years, Wars
and other circumstances had delayed its intro-
duction into Parliament; but, in the mean-
while, it had been much discussed. The form
in which it was at last presented was the
result of arrangements between the Crown and
the Deputies, with a view to make it as little
unpalatable as might be to the House by
which it has been contumeliously kicked out.
That spirit of conciliation or of compromise,
as different persons differently view it, has
been exhibited in vain. The event may show
the futility of attempts to gain over interests
at variance with national welfare; but what
has been lost in the yielding will be got back
by the recoil. Had the proprietary Chamber
been divided in opinion on the subject, and
had the measure been negatived by no very
large majority, the case would have been
otherwise than it is; but since, in a Chamber
consisting of 163 members, no fewer than 140
voted No, the case is evidently that of a house
of legislature utterly out of tune with the
prevailing sentiment of the nation, which is
judge of the matter in the last resort.
We need not trouble our readers with any
attempt at an exact description, either of the
insurgent Chamber as it now exists, or of the
Bill which has excited its rage to so high a
pitch. Enough to say generally, that the
materials of which the former is composed
are high and mighty; but more high in their
own conceit than they are mighty in any
substantial respect; and that tho towing

of the latter was, in a timorous spirit
almost inviting a kick, to pare down a
little the eminence of privilege on which the
Chamber and its individual members stand in
their respective
,counties and in the capital.
The fact is, that a petty nobility ought to be
far more cautious in the use of its advantages
if it would have them to be lasting; whereas,
these Prussian squires, as one may call them,
have contrived to make themselves odious to
very large, and what should be, influential
sections of the community. The instructed-
ness of the Germans as a nationality has been
slow to feel its feet and to assert its claims ;
but, let a just:confidence be once entertained,
and a resolute stand be taken, and these small
landholders will be swept away (politically
speaking) like the chaff of the summer
thrashing-floor.

One of the efforts of the Bill in question
was, so to enlarge the peasant and townsman
elements in the country assemblies as that, in
the choice of the Landrath, which was to be
given to them, their voices should be in some
measure a counterpoise to the heretofore un-
restrained tyranny of the big and little lords
of the soil. The pill was gilded with some
provisions favourable to the landlord interest,
but altogether insufficient to stop their rising
wrath.

It will be their wisdom, however, to observe
that the measure was far from satisfying the
real view of the Liberal party in Parliament
and in the country. One portion of them
supported it as not without some good in
itself, and as an aoknowledgment, at least,
of the existence of such a party in the State,
but another portion declined, thinking it the
better policy to give more rope to an un-
teachable class who will be all the surer to
hang themselves. It remains to be seen bow
the EMPEROR-KING will be advised by his
ehrevici and prompt adviser to deal with the
difficulty. Prince BISAILROIC has not yet ap-
peared upon the scene, and in his absence it
Is not obscurely hinted that what we call a
creation of new peers will be had recourse to,
in order to make sure of a ministerial majority
in the House of notables. This, of course,
has little to recommend it beyond its suffic-
ing for the nonce. No cure, it is not even
a palliative. On the contrary, viewed aright
it is one blow more at the root of hereditary
legislatorship. You must either have no
second Chamber at all, or your second Cham-
ber must as certainly, though under a diffe-
rent mode of ascertainment, be expressive of
public opinion as the first. Then, and then
only, will be realised whatever benefits the
existence of two houses can confer without
that hopeless clashing which here, as in
Prussia, too often threatens to stop, if not to
shatter, the whole political machine.

LORDS.

IN 1835 Mr. ROEBUCK published a pamphlet
entitled "Of what Use is the House of Lords ?"
It need not be stated here that the opinions
expressed in this are very different from those
of his Sheffield speech last week, wherein he
praised this same assembly in a way more
remarkable for warmth of expression than new-
ness of idea. In his earlier utterances his con-
demnation was heavy, direct, unhesitating.
few passages transcribed literally will show
better than anything we might say what
Mr. ROEBUCK thought of the assembly which
he praises so loudly to-day thirty-seven
years ago. "They are as cruel as they dare
be, and meaner than they are they could not
be." "Of their ignorance it is hardly neces-
sary to speak. That has become a bye-word
and a proverb." "When an error has been
exploded from every other nook in the king-
dom, lit still finds a sanctuary in the House of
Lords." "Every amelioration in the condition
of the people, every improvement in their
institutions, has been made in spite of the
House of Lords, and not with their assistance."
"All that is base, all that is mean, all that is
eorrapt, all that is cruel in our various insti-
tutions flies to the Lords for succour." "Each
dying abuse contributes to the well-being of
the nation; but the sinister interests of the
Hoye of Peers suffer in proportion. The
fence that is put round the pockets of the
•
people keeps out the pilfonng 414 ot the

rapacious and idle noble." "The Lords have
a direct interest in fleecing the people—in
other words, in bad government." "So far
as the House of Lords being more worthy,
more instructed than the Commons, it is im-
measurably inferior to it in everything that
is requisite to constitute an efficient and
worthy legislative body." "My opinion then
is, that the influence of an aristocracy upon
the manners, morality, and intelligence of a
nation, is one of unmixed and enormous evil."
An aristocracy "embitters all the social rela-
tions of life, renders society one continued
strife and contest for superiority, induces
habits of injurious expense, creates suspicion
between individuals and classes, and thus
makes our manners the most fatal enemy to
our happiness."

These aere written, not spoken, opinions,
published when Mr. RoEnuex was thirty-four
years old, and by no means a tyro in political
discussion. They are extreme opinions it is
true, but they are expressed with a strength,
and put forth with a deliberateness of aim
which leave no doubt that they were well
and carefully thought out before they
were uttered.; and a considerable number
of other passages quite as strong in thought
and expression might bo strung on the same
bead-roll as the above, were it at all necessary
for the purpose we have in view.

Now, in contrast to these, very little can be
taken from the Sheffield speech. It was not
long or laboured, a fact that may be set down
as a boon to the Cutlers, inasmuch as it was
very common-place and dull. It was of the
operative Conservative typo of talk, meant
simply to tickle the ears of easy believers.
He commenced by saying that calling him up
to propose the House of Lords was a sort of
"delicate irony." It was, however, more than
that, it seemed rather like a vulgar and cruel
practical joke, which instead of countenancing
he ought to have resented., especially as he
must have felt how little he had to say, and
how painful that little would have been to
any man of ordinary sensibility of mind, so
far committed as the honourable gentleman was
to the "other side." We presume, however,
under the ciroumstanoes, he did the best he
could. He declared that in giving his former
opinions "he had been mistaken." His opinion
now is that the House of Peers is "a body of
men who represent property and influence as
distinguished from the House of Commons,
whioh directly represented the people "—that
"it is the wisest checking power that could be
devised for society so peculiarly constituted as
ours."

This is the sum total of the praise so far as
we can gather it, and that this was delivered
without any hope of a bribe from the Peers of
England it is very easy to believe, even
without Mr. ROEBUCK'S declaration that "No
one who possessed the wildest imagination
could suppose that ho praised the House of
Lords because he expected anything from
them now," or his additional statement that
his favourable opinion was not connected
"with personal interest."
It is almost certain that nobody will suspect
that Mr. ROEBUCK is on the look out for a
title. Baron TEAREM would sound well enough,
but an honour so earned could not be of much
value to Mr. ROEBUCK himself; and that the
dignity or usefulness of the House of Peers
could be much increased thereby can hardly
be conceived by the "wildest imagination."
As regards his motives, Jouri- ARTHUR
ROEBUCK may make his mind perfectly easy.
It is scarcely credible that any man in England
would trouble his head to discover them. At
one period of his life there was hope in con-
nection with his labours; it is not so now.
The public man who, at the ripe ago of
seventy-one, has no better work than that of
self-correction, especially one who has been a
political sinner for so long a period as Mr.
ROEBUCK, has more than enough to occupy
him for the remainder of his days. Could Mr.
ROEBUCK live an additional thirty-five years
he might find his way back to where he stood
five-and-thirty years ago, and from that point
commence anew the work from which he has
taken his hands, and by consistent efforts
atone for the follies he has committed. As
things stand, the wortig - acts cf Mr.

ROEBUCK have no more interest for the general
public than those of an itinerant quack.
What Mr. ROEBUCK is really aiming at is,
we imagine, sufficiently obvious. He desires
to be once more returned for Sheffield, and he
knows that his old Liberal friends can never
be brought to satisfy that desire. He has,
a hold upon a considerable number of
people by his ability, as well as by his long
connection with the borough ; and if to these
he can add such Tories as may hate the com-
parative extremeness of Mr. MUNDELLA, or as
may be taken in by his eulogium on the
House of Lords, he may attain the object he
has in view. Amongst our great trading
magnates there are two classes likely enough
to support him, provided they cannot procure
the return of a thorough-going Conservative,
namely, those who regard Toryism as almost
necessarily a rich or respectable man's
political creed, and those who, though pre-
tended Liberals, yet believe that extreme
opinions and rapid political changes are
dangerous to the owners of property. That Mr.
ROEBUCK may be returned by a union of
such parties is likely enough, if the working
men of Sheffield do not make their minds
thoroughly up to prevent it; and that an injury
to the Liberal cause may come in this way is
quite possible, but whatever happens in this
matter one thing is certain, namely, that Mr.
ROEBUCK'S political career has finished. For
the future, either in Parliament or out of
Parliament, he never can:do good or harm.
Through personal vanity, impracticability of
temper, violent invective, and glaring self-

articles.title: 301 IN STUART MILL AND THE INTERNATIONAL.
articles.text:
301 IN STUART MILL AND THE
INTERNATIONAL.

Jonx Srianr MILL'S letter to the SECILETA.RY
of the Nottingham Branch of the Interna-
tional Working Men's Association 'claims
the consideration of thoughtful Liberal
politicians. That there is such an organiza-
tion as the "International" none of us can
doubt, whatever opinion we may entertain of
its numbers or influence. But for many
reasons besides that pointed out by Mr.
MILL it is desirable that exaggerated notions
of its importance should not be encouraged.
Look at it how we may, we always see in it
a preponderance of foreign thought and speech,
which prevents us from regarding it otherwise
than as a weakly exotic which never can take
root and flourish on English soil.
The lecture given by Mr. MILL to the per-
sons who forwarded him their International
pamphlet, entitled "The Law of the Revolu-
tion," is well-timed and exceedingly appro-
priate. We know of no such thing as "the
Revolution' belonging to the present or the
future of England, nor do we want to have
paraded before us any indefinite phrase which
excites alarm without possessing meaning or
purpose. The correspondence of which Mr.
MILL'S letter forms a part has no connection
with, and we may add, has no direct interest
for the masses of English working men, who,
whatever else they may be,
.are not members
of the international Society, and never can
sympathise with a movement which, whatever
its definite objects—if it really has any definite
thought in it—so far as it has gone has found
its chief success in compromising and dis-
crediting the cause of Liberal progress in
England.

In truth its language betrays its origin. It
is not in its organisation, its objects, or its
phraseology really English. Its most active
spirits cannot
,be Englishmen capable or
understanding ideas of progress connected
with the . country, or expressing them as
earnest, thoughtful Englishman, would. The
working men of England know what they
want, and can express themselves in relation
to their wants in their native language. It
would be no difficult matter to name every
question that at the present moment occupies
the thoughts of English working men, Trades
unionism is an absorbing thought, with good
practical work allied to it, but no sensible
%mid Oink 94 eallisig it "the maw.

tion." Co-operation engages the serious atten-
tion of tens of thousands of working men, and
although it may be regarded as the commence-
ment of a mighty change, the man who called
it "the revolution" would be laughed at. We
want still a thorough recasting of our repre-
sentative :system, but people would as :soon
think of calling such a change the "ticket,"
the "go," or the "cheese," as they would of
calling it "the revolution." We require froin
the root up an improvement it . our land laws,
and those who oppose this will call it " spolia-
tion," " flat burglary," and all else that may
be discrediting, but men friendly,: to the
change, because they believe it will be of ad-
vantage to the nation, will;net play into their
opponent's hands by calling it "the Revolu-
tion.''

The working men of England, as a rule,
are sensible men, influenced in their conduct
by their own thought, governed by their own
sense of right, anxious for the welfare of their
country, and, therefore, content to speak their
own language, and act for themselves.

We find no fault with those working men
in England who seek to promote a common
understanding between the working classes
throughout England and America for indus-
trial purposes, or even so far as they can
safely do it, for the purpose of promoting
political and civil liberty. But we are certain
that not one of these objeots can be promoted
by entering into the entanglements of foreign
politics. Our sympathies should be every-
where with the right, but our efforts are due
at home. We can do best that which we
know best, and we ought to remember that
by helping the cause of progress at home we
help it all the world over. There is no violence
includel in the English working man's pro-
gramme. He has discovered how much more
potent and enduring in its influence thought
is, and how much more desirable the peaceful
labour is that gives it form and substance.
It is to be hoped, therefore, that no ono will
suppose that those few men who aim at doing
everything in general, but nothing in particu-
lar, and who express their objects in a half
understood foreign jargon, will not be mistaken
for the working men of England, who think
English thought, speak English words, and
work in a true and downright English fashion,
for tho purpose of abolishing such abuses of
law and custom, as lie within their power to
understand, and within their duty to attack
and destroy.

RE-ELECTION OF PRESIDENT GRANT.
TILE single fact of the week is the defeat
of Mr. GREELEY and the consequent re-election
of General GRANT to the Presidentship of the
United States. The triumph is overwhelming
to the unsuccessful candidate, who, they say,
resumes the editorial pen, promising support to
the reforms of his vietorious competitor, and for.
swearing all attempts at office for the future.
Since the elections in October, Mr. GREELEY
was deemed sure to lose, but nobody expected
him to be so ridiculously behind. The event
shows a prevailing gratitude for the military,
services of the honoured man, and, as to
trust in him, a reliance upon his character
if not upon anything very remarkable
in his statesmanly abilities. In another
four years, however, he may, by wise conduct,
add a political to a warlike fame. His
countrymen know that he has persistency and
perseverance; and no President need be at a
loss for the best advice and assistance that a
population of forty millions can afford him.
The four years last passed have been his ap-
prenticeship to the art and science of govern-
ment; the four to come will enable him to
show what proof he can of proficiency. In all
probability, now that the exigency that makes
a man acquainted with strange bedfellows is
over, even Mr. GREELEY will not quarrel with
such legislation as re-affirmed in the South the
s
moral and social conquests of the Civil 'War.
Perhaps it is as foreigners that we Briton view
the commercial and financial acts of General
GRANT'S first term of office. His own country ,
men cannot but rejoit over the steady-reduc-
tion of their national dot, and the consequent
restoration of their national credit; and ho
has before him the happy prospect of with one
hand reducing the burdens of the taxpayer
and with the other refaildiug borrowedszoney.

.4, foreign. matters, he has been almost unex-
ceptionally fortunate. If he failed to annex
S. Domingo, he kept out of danger with
,respect to Cuba; and, while preserving strict
neutrality betwixt France and Germany, he
has made a large gain for his country at the
same time that he has united with England
in aiming the heaviest blow at international
rar that has ever fallen upon the head of that
hateful monster. Much, too, is he to be con-
gratulated upon the peaceful no less than
decisive triumph now given him by tho votes.
of his fellow citizens. The Republic of the
United States has on this occasion covered
itself and its constitution with true glory and
honour.

FRIENDLY SOCIETIES AND TRADES'

UNIONS.

Mr. Stephenson, the Registrar of Friendly
Societies in England, reports that be received
10,795 returns this year from the societies, and
that those which state the number of members in
1871, show a total of 1,589,176, and those
which state the amount of funds allow a total
of £8,026,894. In the year 1871 the
Registrar examined and certified the rules
of 1,045 friendly societies, and registered 56
industrial and provident (or co-operative) societies.
He received notices of the dissolution of 63
friendly societies, the majority of which were
probably in a condition of virtual insolvency;
and he advertised in the Gazette agreements for
the dissolution of 76 other societies, whose trustees
thus secured a statutory discharge from liability.
In the case of many, or most, of these last the
cause of dissolution was not insolvency, but merely
a determination on the part of the members to dis-
tribute the accumulated funds. In one-fourth of
these cases the funds divided exceeded £lO per
member. One was a female benefit society,
established at Stockton in 1800 by a philanthropic
lady; by donations from her husband and others,
and the payment of members, the funds have so
accumulated that the members, now only 22, some
of them of great age, will be comparatively
enriched. One, a woman of 83, whose payments
in 60 years have amounted to only £24, will
receive, in lieu of the is. 6d. a week to which she
would be entitled, a sum of nearly- £lOO down.
This is not the result contemplated by the benevo-
lent ladies who interested themselves in the
formation of the society 70 years ago, but the
members have a right to agree upon a dissolution.
The Registrar also, as barrister under the Savings
Baas Act, certified in the year the rules of 117
benefit building societies, of 47 loan eocieties, and
of eight literary societies, the certificate granted to
these last exempting them from the payment of
local rates.

.Mr. Stephenson is also Registrar of Trades'
Unions under the Act of PlB7l, and in that capa-
city he registered two Trades' Unions in 1871—
viz., the Operative Bricklayers' Society (London)
with funds amounting to £4,664, and income of
£1,655 and 1,441 members; and the Warehouse-
men's Philanthropic Society (Bradford), with funds
amounting to £1,969 and an income of £354. In
1871 ho registered 27 Trades' Unions; seven of
them, having been in existence more than a year,
have made returns which show at the end of 1871
they had in the aggregate funds amounting to
£19,990 and an annual income of £21,593, and
live of them had 10,091 members. At the com-
pletion of this report about 50 other applications
for registration only awaited compliance with the
requirements of the Act; these are very clearly set
forth in the form of applications for registry pre-
scribed by the Secretary of State, but not a single
Trade Union complied with all of them on first
sending its rules to the Registrar. Two applications
were refused on the ground that the object dis-
closed in the rules did not comprise any of those
declaseci by the Act to be objects of a Trade
Union. In the instance of the Amalgamated
Society of Carpenters and Joiners it appears that
differences had arisen between the executive council
in London and the general council in Manchester,
most of the branches supporting the latter, but
some adhering to the former; both parties made
application for registration under the above title,
and the Registrar refused to register either. On
appeal the Court of Queen's Bench held that he
was right. One of the rules made under the Act
directs that no Trade Union be registered under
the same name as that of another Union.

THE LONDON SHIP-BUILDERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-Myr.
Sra,—lt is with feelings of the deepest
regret that we have cause to inform you, and
through the oolutnus of your valuable and
widely-read paper, to inform the public, that
we, the workmen in Messrs. Dudgeon's ship-
building yard, Cubitt Town, Poplar, have felt
it our duty as men to respectfully decline the
appointment of a thorough tyrant to till the
responsible situation of bub-manager in the
above mentioned yard.
Sir, the person chosen for that office is so
well and so widely known in every ship-
buildinae-yard on the river, that it would be
a work of supererogation on our part to say a
word upon the subject.
But to those of your readers who feel in-
terested in the trade, and who are not inti-
mately acquainted with the shipbuilding
trade of the river, it may not be out of place
to state that the person employed as sub-
manager has, for the last nineteen years, been
known as one of the most determined tyrants
ever known in the experience of any workman
on the river.
There is no man safe. If he has ever come
across any man who had a spark of manly

self-respect in him, he has either driven that
thoroughly out, or driven the man from the
yard to starve, for what he cared.
The poet Gray says, in his immortal Elegy,
"Some village Hampden, who with dauntless
breast,
The pretty tyrants of his fields withstood."
Sir, we have had nampden's in plenty, but
I am sorry to say they had to go to the
wall.

As we said before, they must either as men,
relinquish their own self-respeot, or leave the
work; and where a man has a wife and family
dependant upon him, it is not every man who
can enact the part of a Hampden.
One of our principal reasons for wishing the
public at large to know the reason of the
difference with our employers is emphatically
as follows :

That ceasing work upon the reasons given,
we feel the exceeding delicacy of our position.
We feel how easy it would be to represent
that we would dictate to our employers who
they should or should not employ to manage
their business.

Now, sir, we most decidedly affirm that we
have no wish to da so. That to a man we
have the very highest respect and esteem for
our employers, and would assure you that we
will not soon forget the gentlemanly and
considerate manner in which they granted us
the nine hours without being asked for it.
With these feelings to our employers, and
with our feelings towards the person he has
employed as sub-manager, you. and your
readers will see that we have a delicate duty ;
in short, as Desdemona says, we have a
decided duty.
We, as men, having the utmost respect
for our employers, we have still the duty of
respecting ourselves, which by years of
ex
perience we know to be simply impossible
under the rule of the appointed sub-manager.
As men, and as workmen, we feel con-
strained to say, that the Messrs. Dudgeon
have been ill-advised to appoint such an
obnoxious person to fill such a very re-
sponsible situation.
Signed, ROBERT HEIMERSON, President,
Committee Rooms, Newcastle Arms, Cubitt
Town, Poplar, E.

THE LABOUR REPRESENTATION
LEAGUE AND THE FENIA.NS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

SlR,—The reasons which have been put for-
ward by the Government for keeping the men in
prison aro not of sufficient force to justify their
detention. It is true that some Of these men
were under special allegiance as soldiers in
Her Majesty's service, and this, no doubt,
might be regarded as an aggravation of their
offence; but still they were Irishmen, acting
nn.der what they, no doubt, believed to -be
-motives of the highest patriotism, and were
subject, like other men, to be swayed by the
prevailing national excitements. Let it be
remembered, too, that the emissaries of the
Government, when employed' in the detection
of the Fenian conspiracy, were—as came out
in certain of the trials—industrious 'in draw-
ing men into it, thus entrapping unwary per-
sons in order to make profit by their convic-
tions. _ _ _ _ _

The past treatment of Ireland by English
Governments has been of the very worst kind,
and the acts for whioh the Fenian prisoners
wore suffering ought to be looked at in
connection with their exciting cause.
Theirs is a very common form of offence.
Every oppressed nation in the world has
been the theatre of such breaches of the
law, and in such oases history and experience
alike prove that a wise leniency is a better
policy for effecting conciliation than harshness
and severity. Fortunately at present there is
a disposition on the part of the Government of
England to act justly, towards Irelana, and
even were this not the ossa the sympathi4 of
the English people, Veito irronow:-4e itTemem-
bered--Linfluentiiil in 'otir own legislation, will
prevent, I believe for ever, the reourrenee
of those acts of disgraceful oppression which
have been the fruitful source of the discontent,
suffering, and disturbance, which have hitherto
stood so much in the way ef Ireland's prosperity
and progres. The masses of our English
people wish well to Ireland, and the blessings
involved in this will soon become apparent if
their good-will be relied on with generous
confidence by the Irish people. Oppression in
the past, though in different degrees, has been
common to the people of both countries, and
by studying the lesson this teaches they may
each secure justice in the future by mutual
friendliness and trust: Let Irishmen, there-
fore, look more to the future, in which there
is hope of good; and less to the past in which
they find so much to occasion anger and. dis-
like, and let them never forget that the
oligarchic Government, under which they
suffered wrong, is gradually giving place to a
popular Government, under which like wrong
—or intention of wrong of any kind—cannot
be enacted. Lt them remember also that a
union of heart, as well as of law between the
peoples of both nations, cannot be a degrada-
tion or oppression for Ireland, and that of such
a union, local legislative life may come to her
in a way beneficial to the whale Empire.
I say) unhesitatingly, there 10 up good or

useful purpose to be served by keeping these
i
men shut up in prison. It sto be hoped,
therefore, that they will be liberated, and that
for the future the people of England and
Ireland may so respect and trust each other as
to render wholly impossible acts of conspiracy
and insurrection on the one side, or, of
severity in punishment on the other. The
popular mind has ceased to believe in need-
less severity, and as the liberation of the
Fenian prisoners could scarcely fail to con-
ciliate a large number of active sympathisers
in Ireland and elsewhere, I sincerely trust a
favourable ear will be turned to the cry for
an amnesty now so earnestly raised.
Very faithfully yours,
R. MARSDEN LATIUM,
President of the Labour Representation
League.

FREE TRADE IN LAND.

In an article on the question of land tenure
by Mr. Arthur Arnold, in November num-
ber of the Contemporary ocour the
following passages :
Eight yearS'ago, in a vast mill-shed erected
by the co-operative enterprise of working men,
I listened to the last public words of Richard
Cobden. Never have I seen greater homage
Paid to living man. Some rough deal planks
formed a sounding-board above his head ; the
place was not well lighted; his words could
reach but little more than half the vast
assembly. Five or six thousand people had
congregated to listen to the unadorned' elo-
quence of this practical man in a 'place most
bare of ornament. He spoke with the measured
tone of one who is sensible of great responsi-
bility, as a man ought to speak whose words
were carried to the magic needles ere the ink
that recorded them was dry, and flashed away
to all the great centres of English intelligence,
there to be reproduced a thousand times before
the eyes of his countrymen. That night he
offered to the competition of English statesmen
a splendid prize—the rich guerdon of a merit
brighter than his own; a reward nobler even
than that respect betokened by the myriad of
.upturned faces hanging, as it were, with un-
questioning confidence upon his words. He
expressed his belief that success would attend
a properly conducted effort to establish free
trade in land; and be asserted that the man
who should aceomplish this work will have
done more for the English poor than had been
effected by the application of free trade to
commerce. And there it lies; the prize fell to
the ground; death sealed the lips of the
speaker; his words have assumed the solem-
nity of a bequest but nothing, positivity
nothing has been done towards the establish-
ment of free trade in land. I really do not
believe that any one possessed of great in-
fluence in the Legislature questions the bene-
ficial influence which a free exchange of land
would exert. "We Englishmen," as Kr.
Gladstone said at Greenwich, "who have
' received from Mr. Cobden a special Commis-
sion and a special charge," have strangely
neglected our calling. Believing in their
utterances, it can only be supposed that the
conscientious men who direct the powers of the
State have been waiting long years for a
favourable breath of public opinion and for a
clear channel. . . . I say the time has
come when this tacit submission to the landed
monopoly •exists no 'longer ;Iwhen the main-
tainers of the present land system Must fiodept
refer& or risk the incln chances of revolUtian.
Slowly but surely the people are mastering
this question. Every wind that blows brings
to the shores of England testimony to her
matchless wealth and to her unequalled
poverty. Englishmen know, as a rule, very
little of other countries; and the books•which
have been written are, for the most p:irti very
superficial, or trio" dry" Mr popular • reading,
But they are aWare that btu. -land Spit*, to
far as it is known 'abroad,' excites the wonder
rather than the admiration of the world: There
are countifes of peasant proprietors, like France,
Switzerland, and Belgium; there are other
lands with a class analogous to our landed
aristocracy; but there is no other portion of
the earth where the land is for the most
part owned by one -class, farmed by
another, and tilled by, a third, . .
I am no alarmist; yet .1 sincerely believe it
would be dangerous for the landea interest to
set its face against reform. To what could
they trust in such -a policy? The forbearance
of the now all-powerful people? Why should
these exercise forbearance? Does history read
such a lesson to the people About two hun-
dred years ago the position in which the land.
owners and the people find themselves to-day
was reversed ; the former were mightiest in
Parliament. And what did they do? They
found a large taxation levied on the land of
which it is not untrue to say that it was the
purchase-money of their estates ; they threw
off these feudal dues, and substituted and Act
"that the people of England should pay a tax
of is. 3d. per barrel on all their beer and ale,"
with a proportionate sum on all other liquors
sold throughout the kingdom. And it WAS
enacted that a moiety of this tax "shall be
settled on the Ring's Majesty, his heirs and
:successors, in full recompense and aatistaotion
ifor all tenures in capito and by knight service,

and of the courts of wards and liveries, and all
emoluments thereby weaning, and in full
satisfaction for all purveyance. ' This Ad was
carried in a House of three hundred Members
by a majority of two. Then again, when' a
land-tax of 4s. in the pound had been imposed,
the landowners contrived, in. 1697, so to frame
the tax (9 Wm. lII.' c. 10) that it ehoild not
increase with the value of the land, as was at
first intended, but should be a fixed annuity
without rise in value, I do not bring forward
these things as charges against the landed in-
threst—they are now merely historical—nor do
I refer to them as incentives to those whose
ancestors paid so dearly for the legislation of
the Caroline period. 1 hope the people will
use their power wisely and fairly; but I have
yet to see a party which, being in undisputed
possession of authority, has been uninfluenced
by motives of class interest. I refer to these
things as a warning to the landowners, sug-
gesting their acceptance of such moderate,
such wholly advantageous reforms as those I
have sketched in the friendly spirit in which
they are framed. When Cobden said, in 1845,
" I warn the aristocracy not to force the People
to look into the subject of taxation; not to
force them to see how they have been robbed,
plundered, and bamboozled for ages by them,"
he spoke in days very far removed, in reference
to political affairs, from our own. • Were ho
with us now, he would be the first to admit
this; but I am very sure that he would de-
mand free trade in land ; and, if it were with-
held, he would not fail to arouse the people to
a sense of their tights in this respect.

Vottifi Grua,*

WHAT IS LOYALTY?

What is loyalty P is it to cringe and crawl,
Like crouching curs in some unlucky hour;
To lick the feet of princes, and to fall
In base idolatry before established power?

Is it to tremble at the haughty breath
Which leaves the lips of those of royal blood;
To act as though their ireful glance were death,
And their bland smile the sole, the sovereign
good?

Is it to cleave the air with shouts; to cry
Like supple slaves, "Long live our gracious
King;"
Though outraged truth strip bare the shameless
And in our teeth his graceless actions fling ?
If this is loyalty, men should withhold
Their heart's free tribute from such senseless
fraud;
Nor place, nor power, nor tfireat, nor tempting

golds -
Should move free lips till love and truth ap-
plaud.

"The right divine of kings," is an old plea,
Urged in excuse by many a grovelling throng;
Bight is divine, and evermore shall be,
But kings have often reign'd by charter'd
wrong.

The meanest toiler horn, to sweat and groan
Beneath the yoke of labour and of care,
Has rights as sacred as a monarch's own,
Though Go alone may listen to his prayer.
True loyalty Jives in the grateful heart,
Which will not grudge a generous mod of
praise,
To kings, who act through life a kingly part,
And leave their deeds to shine in after days.
But if they bring dishonour on the crown,
And stain the royal purple with their crimes;
Should men shame honesty, cause truth to frown,
By raising shouts to suit the venal times?

Men may respect their country and their kind,
And spurn the hand that draws the rebel blade ;
Yet scorn to bend in adoration blind,
Or flaunt themselves in frivolous parade.
We ne'er should teach our rulers to forget,
That all are subjects of the "King of Kings,"
That human suns oft at meridian set,
And highest honours wear the lightest wings.
Kings should be guardians of the people's laws,
They are not fountains whence all virtues flow;
Princes and kings have many ugly flaws,
As sad experience and all history show.
Loyalty is fidelity to Right,
i Love s its root, and truth its comely crown ;
When Wrong misgoverns with the rod of Might,
The face of flight must frown the monster
down.

They are most loyal who oppose tho most
The scourges of their country; these are they,
Who in the vanguard of fair freedom's host,
Chock both rebellious and despotic sway.
NOA.II COOKE.
Kidderminster.
