THE OLD PLAYER'S STORY.

I once embraced the offer of an intelligent
master of a workhouse to visit the establishment
under his charge. Ile received me at the door,
and led me through the various rooms. The
occupants were nearly all old men, a few—very
few.—were younger and sickly-looking, all dressed
alike in the gray suit, and looking all alike, in a
sullen and hopeless expression that is very sadden-
ing to see on human faces. Of course I asked
questions by the score, and was answered. Few
of them liked to discuss the cause of their ending
their days in that place. Some few said it WM
misfortune; some said—poor old fellows—that
their children had died; some did not know
exactly what it was had brought them there.
They had very little bread whore they were, they
said; and the master smiled.
"You've enough to eat, Brown r
"Yes. I don't starve, but somehow I never
feel full, always waiting for next meal; itain't
pleasant sort of feeling that; still I can't help it,
I am here, and shall be till I goes."
The twit word was half regretful, half expectant
in its tone.
"Ile is a fair sample of your birds, I suppose,"
said L

"Yes, about the average, perhaps a little better
than the &morel runS I'ye rather tcita spool-

men here somewhere. I like the old fellow, his is
a sad case. Where's Gowling ?"
"He is in the garden, Sir," said one. "Ye
can just see him out of the window here, Sir,
sitting under the lime-tree, there ;" and a finger a
little, just a little dirty, was stretched out to
indicate the place of Gowling.
I of course looked, and saw a man I should
have judged to be about sixty-five sitting under
the tree. He was a good deal bent, and seemed
lost in thought from the wrinkles on his face, or
it might have been the vacant smile I had seen on
other faces, though I could hardly tell what it was
at that distance.

On my going up to him, the old man rose, and
took off his cap with a grace and ease of manner,
and withal a certain dignity, that made me
instantly raise my hat.
"Would you like to sit down, Sir?' said no;
and he looked at me.

"Thank you," I stammered, and sat down. I
had not recovered from my astonishment—the
pauper, with his cap that never could have cost
sixpence, exhibiting with it the manners and ease
of a gentleman. I was astonished, and bat
silent.

"You've been through the house ?"
" Oh, yes—l went through this afternoon."
"Curious place. Curious people in it."
" Yes ; but they are all much alike in the main
features, dress of course—but manner, expression
of face. Most of them are from the same class,
the labouring poor,' as one of our poets has em-
phatically called them. You find them not very
congenial companions r _

"-Not very.. .They are kind, or mean to be; and.
would be respectful, if there were not adverse in-
fluences to the existence of such a feeling. The
chaplain is rather against me."
"You smoke, Mr. Gowling
"I do, when I can," and the old man laughed—
a laugh that was at once bitter and pitiful.
I offered him my cigar-ease. He made his selec-
tion, and struck a light with the fusee. I lit my
own with one, and was enjoying the first few whiffs,
when I presently noticed my companion's cigar
had no light—it had gone out. I looked in the
fusee-box—it was empty.
"Oh, never mind. I'll keep it till another time."
I handed him mine.

"No, Sir—it's no use to me. My lungs are not
what tkey used to be, and I can't light it unless
you draw at the same time. I can light it then."
I drew my breath till the end of my cigar was
almost a flame, and then the old man, with his
feeble breath, kindled his own. I noticed him
more as our faces were close together. ills brow,
rather high and rounded, was crossed in every di-
rection by wrinkles; the eyes were dark, the eye-
brows almost gone; while the cheeks more
resembled parchment than aught also. The face
close shaven, and a few locks of thin grey hair
just showed under the cap.
"Well," said ho, after some few puffs at his
cigar, "what do you think of me ?"
I. was blushing again. I really thought he had
been too much occupied with his cigar to observo
how much I noticed him.

"I scarcely know. It is so unusual to find one
having your education in such a place as this that
I am sure I hardly know what to think of your
being here."
"You talk of my education. What do you sup-
pose I am ?"
"I was going to say an actor, but that—"
"You're right; I am an actor. I am," ho
sighed, " no—l was."
You really interest ma very mach. I should
be glad, very glad—should take it as a favour, if
you would toll me the—the—indeed, the story of
your life. lam very ratioh interested."
"My dear Sir— '
Now I did feel that it was not usual for mon in
the dress of paupers to address the friends of the
master as "My dear Sir."
"My dear Sir, I shall be very happy if I can
amuse you for a little while—l fear it's no use
beginning before tea. I expect the bell to ring
directly. Ah, there it is. Will you come in and
see the carnivora fed, as they used to say when I
was young ?"
I went in with him, arm in arm—how the
paupers did stare to see the old fellow hanging on
my arm I—and then I saw them sitting down at a
long table—and the little wedge of bread and the
smaller one of cheese wore eaten carefully to
spread out the flavour over a long time. I noticed
my companion had a cup of tea brought him, which
was a favour accorded to but few: half an hour
and it was over, and we came out again into the
garden and sat down once more. Hs seemed
revived.

"I like my tea. You see we are not allowed
many stimulants hero, and I only got this every
day by the order of the doctor—a young fellow I
used to know many years ago. I
i was playing
Othello at the time n Bradford, and an accident
having happened to one of the shifters, he was
called in. lie sot his leg—it was broken—and
helped him with money afterwards, I know, and I
took a liking to him. Ile was just beginning to
practise then, and thought it a fine thing to know
an actor. Ile orders me tea now ; " and the old
man was silent.
"Try another cigar, Mr. Gowling, and you'll
be better ; " and ho did. It really was a pleasure
to see him slowly and weakly draw in the smoke,
and then as slowly and weakly let it curl out of
his scarcely opened lips with an air of regret at
its departure. Ile smoked on in Once for some
time and I let him without interruption.
"I said I would toll you my story. Well, to
begin. I was born in this town of Bunton some-
thing less than sixty years ago. My father was a
small tradesman, and sent ma to tho best school
ho could afford till I was a littlo over thirteen.
He was rather proud of niN poor old father. I
used to recite on the public days in the school, and
repeat Latin and Greek orations, of which the
meaning was not a little obscure even to me;
what it must have been to my hearers I don't
know. My father took me away from school to
to shop. Ile was tailpr, 404'4 tl44k any ,

boy with a grain of life in him would choose to be
a tailor as a matter of taste. As for me, it worried
me to death to sit hour after hour, stitch, stitch,
stitch; and I used to beguile the time by reciting
and reading to the few men my father employed,
and they did my share of work in return for the
amusement it afforded them. At the age of fifteen
I took part in some private theatricals in the town,
and found the bustle of preparation much more
pleasant than the dull shop-work. They went off
well, and when next the players came to the town
I went to the manager and asked him to take me.
lle laughed, for I was fit for nothing. Of course
I was too big for a page, and too little for a man-
at-arms, too young for a first, second, or even
third lover, and too old, for any accidental boy
parts. I was disappointed; but I soon had to
leave the then detested shop. My father was
rather of a serious turn. Ile heard of my going
to the manager, and locked me up, then about six-
teen, and fed me on bread and water. This was
rather too bad; so I took French leave, and when
the bread and water came one morning there was
no one to eat it. I was pleased to fiad myself
with a pair of socks awl a clean shirt wrapped up
in a handkerchief, about to face the world, and
try to wring the hard-held honours from stern
fortune's hand.' Still I was young then. I need
scarcely tell you that sitting here I often regretted
that fine May morning's work that took me from
home.

"I went to one town after another, and at each
sought out the manager of the theatre, and tried
hard to get in as anything. I was no use; my
voic3 was not yet sot or certain. 'Why, young
Sir,' said one to me, you're as slim as a girl, and
if you were to make love in the tone you've been
talking to me in, the people would insist that I
had made a girl play the lover's part. I'd take
you, but you are no use to me at all. Two years
hence you can come again—then I may talk to
you.'
"I felt it was true, but still wanted to be in a
theatre; so I entered a travelling circus company
as holder and ring-raker. I kept at it for eighteen
months, and then the manager joined another in
the regular acting line. Now was my chance.
They wanted a lover, and wanted him to ride;
their first lover could no more sit a horse than a
sack could; the first lady ,saw him ones, and said
she should die with laughing if he came on; so I
offered. I did well, and thought I was on the road
to fortune; I folt that Kerable and the rest of the
great actors were only the same men as I was,
with better chances. That is more than forty years
ago though. I'm wiser now.
"After this success I became first gentleman in
that company, and remained so for many years.
The manager took the leading parts, so I had no
chance. 1 changed my name—first, as Gowling
did not look well in a bill; and next, because I
did not want to hurt my poor old father's feelings
more than I could help—l took the name of Al-
phonsus Montague. It looked better on the bills, I
used to think at one time. Somebody, I forget
who, says, 'What's in a name?' I know there is
a good deal in a name when its on the play-bills;
and the public being judge, Alphonsus Montague
was better than ,Tames Gowling, for it drew better
houses.

"In the company there was a girl who took
second lady. I don't say I fell in love with hdr—
I don't think men of our class do fall in love. The
constant exercising the imitative powers in deli-
neating that passion weakens, I think, the power
of feeling it as other men feel it. I liked her; she
was good, industrious, rising in the profession,
and I married her. A better woman never lived
and she had her reward—l don't suppose that
there ever was a woman more respected in any
company. I never had even a row about her but
once, and then, a man being very insolent to her,
she came and told me, just as I came off as Msc-
duff in 'Macbeth.' I went to the manager and
told him that the man must leave the place at
once. The manager said it was impossible; he
was a son of the noble owner of half the Own;
his father was then in the house; these things
must be endured. I said they should not be
endured; and that if he would not protect the
ladies in his company, I should take the liberty of
protecting my wife.'
"And how did it end ?"

"Why, I went to the little beast, titled as he
was, and kicked him out at the stage-door. I did,
Sir, though you would not think it to look at me
now.,,

"And the manager?'
"Came and thanked me. Said he was much
obliged to me; he had had more annoyance from
the complaints of the girls about that fellow than
from any other cause. He raised mine and my
wife's salary that same week."

I had been noticing, while he was speaking, a
number of children who came oat of the house,
and were dispersing in various groups to play.
They were all dressed alike in the gray, true
pauper gray, and ran and jumped as if they were
not dependent on a paternal state for their support.
One child, a little, large-eyed girl, passed ono° or
twice before us, and then stood still, looking at me
a little way off. I looked at her, and she pulled
the corner of her little apron' and blushed, and so
remained till he had done speaking.
"Whose is that pretty child, there ?" said I.
"That—that's my little Alice. Here Alice !
cora° hero, dear."
The child needed no second bidding, but ran to
the old pauper; and, being lifted with no little
effort on to his knee, hid her faca against his
breast, and still glanced atlas. I, of course, found
some object of attraction in the garden that en-
abled me to let her sec my face without my ap-
pearing to see her; she was soon satisfied,
apparently, for the glances became more bold and
determined.

" Who is that, Papa Gowling ?"
"A friend of mine; he won't hurt you."
She looked again to 6013 if I ha I any intention of
doing her mischief, and being satisiled, sat upright
on the old man's knee.

AiiCo ; Yott qeo ho's not going to liurt

my little Alice. Won't you shako hands with
him!"
She did.
"This your grandchild ?" said I.
"Yes,—the only one left," and the voice fell as
he stooped and kissed her uplifted face.
"You were saying that the manager raised your
salary after the little fracas about your wife ?"
"Ah ! yes, ho did, and we went on very well
for some time. I began to find I was not a star.
Once or twice I went up to London and heard
some of the bast men, and found that I could not
equal them. I don't know a more painful sensa-
tion, Sir, than that attendant on the discovery of
the limit of your powers. Every man not blinded
by conceit, who is over thirty, must have felt this.
There is a limit to our powers ; other men have
more—sonic less, but still it is very painful to feel
conscious that the eminence that man has attained
to whom you are listening is beyond you. Young
men—very young men—feel that what man has
done man can do. It thies not last. Most men
at thirty know their pace well enough to tell them
that they will be in the ruck of the race of life.
"Well, some few years after I was married
this conviction came to me—l knew I could never
be a star—a great actor. It was not in me. I
was simply a respectable one. I could take any
part, and do that part so that I was not laughed
at; but there I was stopped. I could go no fur-
ther. I never could raise the enthusiasm of my
audience. They listened and did not disapprove;
but when I played a leading part the boxes did not
let, and the pit was not full. I could not help it,
you know. I can safely say I never went on
without knowing every word of the part. I was
always correct, and in the second and third parts
did well. Stars liked me. They used to come
down for the benefits occasionally, and used to say,
'Let me have Gowling with ma; he's a safe man,
never too forward,—no clap-trap with him—he's
not showy, but he's safe.' Now, you see, praise is ,
a good thing, but when a man has dreamed for ten
years or so that he is to be the star of the theatrical
world, it is rather hard to wake up and find a star
of no very great magnitude telling him he's a very
good back-ground to show that star's light. Ah
me! those hopes of youth—how the largo bud
brings forth but the little flower !"
" Still, Mr. Gowling, it was something not to
have failed utterly. There must be back-grounds,
you know, and there must be second parts as well
as first."

"True, Sir' true; and human natuxo soon
adapts itself to circumstances. Three months
after I knew I was no genius the ambition to be
one left me. I was content to do my part and
enjoy life. I had four children—three boys and
one girl. That's her child—poor little thing."
And he stroked the head of little Alice caress-
ingly while she played with the buttons on his
'Oat.
"The boys, of course, we tried to make useful
in the profession. Chrittmas was a family harvest
—all were busy then—all making money. You
know that the profession is not favourable to health.
The excitement—particularly to children—soon
wears them out. I know, often and often, I've
seen my boys as imps and that kind of thing, and
felt the life was too fast for them. Late at night
to go from the hot theatre into the cold night air
was a sad trial to the constitution, and children
are not old men. You cannot persuade boys of
twelve and fourteen that they ought to wrap their
throats, and not run out into the cold at night.
We could, not, and we lost two of the three buys
within a year of each other. Lung-disease, the
doctor said. It carries off a good many of those
children, you see, in the Christmas pantomimes.
I often wonder whether the house thinks of those
kind of things."

"And the other children ?"
"The boy left our company when he was
about eighteen, and joined another as second
gentleman. He was as good an actor as his father,
and no better. He thought he was a genius, poor
boy, as his father had thought before him. He
had no experience to teach him; so he thou4ht ko
was ill-used and left us."
"And what became of him ?"
"At first we used to hear from him now and
then—then there was a long silence, and his
mother worried herself dreadfully about him. One
night I had been playing a country 'gentleman in
a screaming farce, as the bills called it, for in a
small company you are a king, a warrior, and a
fool—all in one evening; so my wife had gone
home, and when I arrived earae to the doer to lot
me in.
"Don't be frightened, dear, here's Alfred come
back.
"I went up, and there he was; but, my God,
what a wreck I His eyes falood-shot, his hands
trembling, and a hot red spot on his cheeks.
"'Well, father, how are you?
"I did not answer; I sat down and cried. He
tried hard to keep from it, but he couldn't; ho
came and knelt down in front of mo, covered his
face with his hands, and cried like a child. His
mother, poor soul, clung round his nook, and
kissed him, and cried till I was beside myself.
He told his story. He had ma.do a mistake. He
thought himself a great actor. Managers did not;
the public backed the managers, and were right
too. Ile could not stand the disappointment; had
no wife as his father hail had to console him, and
he took to the actor's curse—drink. He sank
lower and lower, became ill, could do nothing,
and just crawled home to die.
"One night, I had just come off, when I was
told some one wanted me at the stage•door.
went, and found. the girl of the house where we
lodged. - She wanted me to come home directly;
I was wanted at once. Mr. Alfred was very

Our manager had his benefit that night, and we
had one of the first-rate London men down
Ha:nlet. I was dressed as the Ghost. I forgot
all about dress then, and rushed 1101113 ; it was too
late, po.A: Alfred was gone! He lay, his head in
his mother's arms; she was dressed as the Qadonf
and was weeping hot, silent tears that fell on iny
dead boy's face, one by one. His sister was Ei!llifc
birnoii hue ktlees by the bod-isido, iv3l ontet`°d

Nov, 9, 1872;

and the people of the house were standing looking
on. I shall never forget it—never.
"I was roused by a touch on the shoulder. A
message from the theatre.
"'Manager says he should be glad if you
could come back.
"'Look here, Jennings, do you think I can ? '
" Not to do anything, Sir; but you might see
him; perhaps it would be better.'
" I left them, and went back, saw the manager
and told him; and though it was his benefit night,
he said he would read both parts himself.
"'God bless you, Gowling, I am sorry for you,
very sorry; if I can do anything for you let me
know.'
"I went to the dressing-room, and as I left the
place heard tho applause that attended the apolo-
gies for our absence, and his announcement of his
intention to read the parts. Managers are not all
alike, and he was a good friend to me, was Charles
Gordon.
"We buried the poor boy, and then went on as
before. His mother never recovered the blow,
and gradually sunk, and about six months after
his death could no longer take her pacts; so Alice
and I had to do our best. I noticed that a young
fellow had been rather attentive to her, and Was
not surprised when he took me aside one night and
told me he wanted to make her his wife. Tie was
just such another as I had been myself whoa his
age. I thought it better to see her the wife of a
respectable actor than remain single behind the
scenes, for she vms a good girl was Alice. Well,
they married, and remained in the company. I
WM getting old you see, then, and it was some
comfort to see her with some one to take care of
her. Soon after she married her mother died, and
laid in the grave, beside her son, one of the beat
'women that ever lived. I was alone now, and
old, for the wear and tear of an active life, and the
late hours, tell on the strongest constitution. It
was something awful the change from the light,
and glare, and noise of the theatre to the, silence
and quiet of my own poor room. Just then, too,
the company was broken up; and at the age I was
then, it was a serious thing for me. We all three
tried to keep together, but it was no use. Those
who wanted an old man did not want a second
lady, or a third gentleman, and so we were divided.
I went on circuit as an old man vi ith very poor
pay—as much as I was worth though, I dare say,
for I was getting feeble, and • Speak up, old 'un
was the salute I had from the galleries directly I
opened my mouth.
"I heard from Alice every week, and saved her
letter for Sundays, for the day was long and dull
to me. I could not make new friends. The young
pitied me, and I was proud then, and 'loved not
pity;' so I was a lonely old man.
"Alice's husband died. I don't remember now
how it was, but he died, and she told me it was
just after this little one washorn. I quite longed
to see her, but she could not come, and I could not
go, so we only wrote to each other. I have all her
letters now, poor girl. She came to see me once
afterwards, and was looking ill and fagged; and
noon after that visit our company was broken up
again.
"I tried hard for an engagement, travelled from
place to plru3e, spent all the little I had saved, and
then was laid up at a plaoe some fifty or sixty
miles from here. They took me from the inn to
the Union when the money was gone; and after a
deal of waiting and grumbling they brought me
here. I little thought when, as a boy, I used to
get the nests out of this tree that I should end my
days here an old worn-out pauper. You know
where it says, There's a Providence that shapes
our ends, rough-how them as we may.' I've often
said that on the stage. I feel it now." And the
old man mused in silence.
"And your daughter ? "
" Alice ? She died in this house not two years

agt?4, poor child."
Here do you mean 1' "
"Yes, there in that room." And he pointed to
a.window in the back part of the house. "That
one, where the sun shines on it through the
trees."
"Of what did she die? She was young."
"The same disease that carried off her brothers,
consumption. She know I was here, and spent
her last money in coming; and the doctor, good
fellow that he is, would have her in here. She
lingered on for about a fortnight up there, and
then died one evening at sunset holding my band,
and the child lying on her breast. Poor girl! she
looked so beautiful in her coffin. Ah ! I've out-
lived them all but this little ono." And the old
man looked fondly on the child, and stroked her
head with his lean shrivelled hand. "It's rather
ead to see them all gone—all—wife sons, and
Alice all gone. Poor Alice ! " And the old
pauper's eyes were full of the slow-coming tears of
age.
I had a cough, and felt husky in the throat, and
the wind blew the dust in my eyes.
"You and my friend seem to agree well, Mr.
Gowling," said the voice of the master close by.
"Yes, Sir, he says he likes to listen to an old
man's talk. It's very kind of him—very kind."
"I've been expressing my wonder to Mr. 0-ow-
ling to find him here."
"Want of proper economy, Sir; nothing more.
People of his profession are very reckless and im-
provident—very."
"You're right and you're wrong at once," said
the old man. "We are not a saving people, I
grant. The whole tendency of the profession is
against it. We don't earn much—l mean such as
myself. Of course genius is always well' re-
warded, but mediocrity in this is subject to com-
petition as in other trades or professions. Then
the little we do earn is spent in ways to which
other professions have nothing analogous. Look
at our dresses—we find all, and when a man
throws himself into his part, does his best to please
the public and do his duty to the manager, he will
not have much left to be extravagant with.
Besides, the qualities of nature that make a good
economist—a careful saving man—are not those
which make a good actor. It is too much to ask
that a man should, on the stage, haye to afoot the

liberal notions of a spendthrift, and off the stage to
be a niggard.
_ _ _

" Still, Mr. Gowling, you admit it is possible to
save."

" Oh, yesl possible, but difficult, inasmuch as
the qualities that make the actor arc not, nor are
they usually found associated with, those of the
rigid economist; and it is only the rigid economist
amOng such men as myself who can save at all.
Look, too, at the liabilities to disease, the uncer-
tainties of the means of living we have, and you
will see that we are, on the whole, as hardly
worked for the amount of pay we receive as any
class of men."

THIRST WORSE TIIAN HUNGER.
That disturbance of the general system which
is known under the name of Raging Thirst is far
more terrible than that of starvation, and for this
reason During abstinence from food the
organism can still live upon its own substance,
which furnishes all the necessary material; but
during abstinence from liquid, the organism has
no such source of supply within itself. Men have
been known to endure absolute privation of food
for some weeks, but three days of absolute priva-
tion of drink (unless in a moist atmosphere) is
perhaps the limit of endurance. Thirst is the
most atrocious torture ever invented by Oriental
tyrants. It is that which most effectnally tames
animals. Mr. Astley, when he had a refractory
horse, always used thirst as the most effective
power of coercion, giving a little water as the
reward for every act of obedience. The histories
of shipwreck paint fearful pictures of the sufferings
endured from thirst; and one of the most appalling
cases known is the celebrated imprisonment of one
hundred and forty-six men in the Black Hole at
Calcutta.

THE ANNUAL OVERFLOW OF THE NILE.
In order to comprehend the power of the trans.
formation produced upon the land by this flood,
the Nile must be viewed at Midsummer, con-
treated, turbid, slimy, stagnant, with black sun-
cracked mud, forming both its shores. AU beyond'
them is sterility and sand, with the forms of
trees, dust-coated and scarce distinguishable,
withering before the Spirit of the Desert. Thus
must Nature lie for a season, that the reinvigora-
ting power of the flood may have opportunity for
beneficence. And lo! its harbinger, the north
ind, cleaving the sandy, burning atmosphere,
makes its presence felt. 'Ale dust disappears, the
colours of Nature shine out again, and all is ex-
peetation of the next great act. It comes at last.
The word is heatd from Cairo that the waters are
rising, and the first green slimy condition of the
augmented stream attests the fact. The green-
ness, however, is soon gone, and the waters wax
more turbid as the tide advances rapidly. They
become at last deep red, like a river of blood,
opaque and thick, throughout Upper Egypt. This
is the Red Nile. The rise goes on now somewhat
fitfully, but incessantly. The thick opaque cha-
racter sometimes partially disappears, but the
deep red hue never, during high Nile, until the
lower lands are reached, by which time much of
the sediment has been deposited. Along the
banks Nature a-tiptoe waits for the welcome flood.
Indefatigably it spreads itself over the burnt face
of the wilderness, and the green herb is percep-
tible once more. Dams burst, and obstructions
are carried away with a mighty noise, but the
sound is not one of torror ; all living things know
it, and rush to meet the kindly power. And yet,
though it comes to bless, its power may be dan-
gerous to the rash or improvident; an ill-fenced
farm or village will be swept away like a lien-
roost; but these are rare accidents. The general
feeling is joy. The men, the children, the buffa-
loes, gambol in its refreshing waters, the broad
waves sparkle with shoals of fish, and fowl of every
wing flutter over them- in clouds. Nor is this
jubilee of Nature confined to the higher orders of
creation—the moment the sand becomes moistened
by the approach of the fertilizing waters, it is
literally alive with insects innumerable. It is im-
possible to stand by the side of one of these noble
streams to see it every moment sweeping away
some obstruction to its majestic course, and
widening as it flows, without fooling the heart
expand with love and joy and confidence in the
great Author of this annual miracle of mercy. By
midwinter the river is again running blue within
its banks.

Did you ever know a child, though dead with
play, who was willing to go to bed? How they
will wink open their poor eyes, and stare about,
and linger round the bright lamps, and plead for a
reprieve, "just a little longer, just five or ten
minutes!" Time will cure them of that soon
enough, poor things, so don't try to teach them the
lesson now. Let them "sit up," before the evil
days come when sleep is the most coveted boon on
earth; when they dread nothing so much as
waking to a new day, and its repetition of weary
struggles with wrong and wrong-doers, lighted
by glimpses of sunshine so few and so transient.
Crowd into the children's insect-life all the little
innocent happiness you can, that they may havo
that at least to look back upon, when they have no
longer the wish or power to " sit up."

Many people-a're-in-tin; habit of mourning over
their ignorance, and complaining because they
have no opportunities for study. If they would

become comparatively well educated. One of the

who had devoted only twenty minutes a day to
study, and had reflected over his reading, as he

person who really wants to become well informed,

MR. WARD BEECH R ON LETTER

WRITING.

Mr. Henry Ward Beecher oloses a characteristic
article in the Netv York Ledger on letter-writing
with the following advice :
Do not begin a letter with an apology or an
explanation. Time is precious. Letters are
multitudinous. Men do not like to open and
clean a letter, like a fish, before they can eat it.
State your business in the trst line. Then, when
you have stated your business, you can go on, if
you wish explanations and apologies, Which the
receiver can read or not, as he pleases. Thus if
one writes "Dear Sir,—l desire to borrow a Thus,
dollars, without interest or security," and
adds eight or ten reasons why, the receiver does
not need to road farther than the first line.
Never begin thus:—" Dear Sir,—You will be
surprised to receive a letter from an entire
stranger," etc. Bless your heart, one now-a-days
is surprised at anything else! Surprised! I am
surprised when Ido not get a pock a week. There
are a few rules which men should commit to
memory, in corresponding with busy people. 1.
Don't write at all. 2. When you can't help it be
sharp, short, and legible. 3. When you write on
your own business, pay for the answer. 4. When
you want money, don't begin with piety or
flattery. Beg first and be pious afterwards. 5.
Don't beg of anyone with whom you are not per-
sonally acquainted. Die, but don't beg.

At the Dartford Poliee-eourt on Saturday,
Sir P. H. Dyke, Bart., in the chair; Richard
Mills and Robert Mills were stuilmoned for

case being called), for the purpose of catching
game. A. gamekeeper had found -a hare on
the Sunday previous, wired, and dead, and
he watched the game in company with another
man. On the following day defendants were
coming along the road and one of them, seeing
the hare, took it up and put it in a bag. The
gamekeepers admitted that the wire was only
two feet from the public road, and that they
did not see the defendants place it where it
was found. Mr,: Oliver, who defended the
accused, said they both bore excellent charac-
ters, and that they bad worked for one gentle-
man for 20 years. As they were proceeding
to their work they saw the hare lying in the
hedge, and one of them took it, but he im-
mediately delivered it up to the gamekeepers.
A witneis was called, who deposed that he
accompanied the defendants to and from work
all the previous week, and knew that no wires
were set , during that time by them. In
answer to the chairman, the defendants said
that their xespective wages were 16s. and 18s.
per week. The ohairmanisaid it was a serious
ease, as the prisoners had no right to touch the
hare, and he fined them Ms. and 10s. costs
e9ch—X6 altogether, or one calendar month's
imprisonment I, Time for payment was re-
fused, and notice of appeal was given.

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

The directors of the Bank of England
yesterday morning decided on the maintenance
of the present rate of discount of six per
cent.

Yesterday morning a fire broke out in the
King's Arms public-house in Sclater-street,
Spitalfields ; several roonis at the back of the
house were entirely destroyed.

The Chief Commissioner has informed the
men, through the divisional superintendents,
that an increased rate of pay would commence
from Monday next; but it was not stated
whether the present scale of pay would .be
revised according to the late demands of the
men,

Lady Auckland, second wife of Baron
A.Ockland, andisecond daughter of the Earl of
Winohelsea, died at Caer House, Doncaster,
yesterday morning. Her ladyship was attacked
by typhoid fever about three weeks ago, and
on Wednesday last coma set in, which, with
effusion on the brain, caused death. She was
only married on the 6th of August last.

Mr. Horace Greeley has resumed the editor-
ship of the New York Tribune on an indepen-
dent basis.

A severe storm visited the North of Eng-
land, Scotland, and Ireland on Wednesday
night, and accounts continue to come in report-
ing the loss and damage occasioned thereby.
In South Shields the most severe westerly gale
experienced for some time oeourred in the
locality. Persons with difficulty were able to
walk in the streets. About nine o'clock several
vessels in Shields harbour broke adrift from
their moorings and were with difficulty brought
up by dropping anchors. The screw steamer
Marian, belonging to London, while entering
the Tyne Dock, came into collision with the
West Pier-bead, drove in her bow, and did
considerable damage to the stonework.
It is probable that the intended new Spanish
loan will be issued about the middle of
December,
In the Senate at bladril, on Wednesday,
the Navigation Treaty. between Spain and the
Netherlands was read. On Friday next the
discussion of the bill for the establishment of
a Mortgage Bank will commence, and Congress
Will remain in session until the vote on this
bill has been taken.

An inquest was held at Leamington on
Wednesday on the body. of Miss ,Ann Bate,
aged 50, who on Monday was found dead
in her bedroom, where there was an empty
bottle which had, contained an ounce of
laudanum. The jury, after much deliberation,
returned a verdict to the effect that the de-
ceased died from a poisonous dose of laudanum,
but there was no evidence to prove whether it
was taken with the intention of committing
suicide, or for the purpose of inducing sleep,
and alleviating pain.
The Cologne Gazette has at, present a cor-
respondent in Paris who is no other than the
Abbe Michaud who lately seceded from the
Church of Rome, and who describes himself as
the Apostate of the Madeline." His letters
are principally devoted to abuse of the
Episcopal Bench in FrOce.

"A marriage, which Makes a great sensa-
tion at this moment," says the Paris Journal,
"is that of the lady who was Princess de la
Moskowa by her father, and Duchess de
Persigny by her husband. In a few days she
will only be the wife of a simple advocate at
Cairo."

estate, at the top of the London-road, Brighton,
fell about eleven o'clock yesterday morning,
burying three men and a boy. The boy, when
extricated, was found to be dead. The men,
who are seriously injured, were removed to
the hospital.

An appeal is made for funds to help the
Orphan Working School, at Haverstock-hill,
which now contains 370 boys and girls who are
taught and trained for domestic and useful
service ; 400 might be admitted but for want
of funds. The secretary is Mr. Joseph Soul,
and his office is at 73, Cheapside.

Mr. G. Cornwall Leigh, the member for
Mid-Cheshire, is seriously ill.

The King of Italy leaves Rome on Saturday
for Naples, and will return on the 20th inst.

Mr. de Conroy, manager of the National
Bank in Tralee, was found dead in bed on
Wednesday morning.

the trial of the Tiohborne Claimant will not
take place dnaing the present term. The
time at the disposal of the Court of Queen's
Bench is limited, and it is currently reported
at Westminster Hall that the prosecution is

Dr. Neilson Hancock's return of criminal
statistica just issued shows that the serious
crimes committed in Ireland last year were
fewer than in any previous twelve months
since 1864. There was a decrease in indict.
able Offences of 14 per cent., as oempared with

Standing Orders for future Trades Union Con.

tiENTLEMBN,—One of the duties which devolved
upon us, as the Parliamentary Committee ap-
pointed at Nottingham in January last, was the
drawing up of Standing Orders for the better
despatch of husi,ness at all future Congresses.
In accordance with the Instructions then received
rca bieig to lay before you the following suggestions,
earnestly requesting that trades societies and
trades councils, or the experienced officers and
members of trades unions, will favour us with
such additional suggestions as their judgment
approves for facilitating the transaction of business
at these annual gatherings.
It is necessary to be borne in mind that these
Congressees are essentially reserved for trades
union delegates, representing bona fide trades
societies, trades councils, and similar bodies, by
whatever name they may happen to call them-
selves; and it is desirable that this fundamental
tharacteristio shall be retained.

--
The only latitude which the Committee recom-
mend is contained in No. 30, which gives the
power to invite persons, not delegates, to attend
the sitt4ngs of the Congress, and, it may be, to
speak, so that those who from time to time identify
themselves with the labour movement, whether in
or out of Parliament, may be able to be present
:to give advice or aid in the great work to which
we have addressed ourselvea.

- -
With these limitations, which have become
eipedient, not in an exclusive spirit, but in conse-
quence of the many important questions to which
we must from time to time devote our attention,
we believe that these annual Labour Parliaments
will rnatsrially aid in giving tone and coherence
to the aspirations of our industrial life, and will
greatly help us in getting such enabling laws
passed by the Legislature, as will be conducive to
the general welfare of the community, not of
sections only, but of all classes of our fellow-
countrymen.

STANDING ORDERS.
1. The Congress shall consist only of delegates
representing One fide Trades Societies, and
Trades Councils, and similar bodies, by whatever
name they may, for the time being, be called.
2. Each delegate shall come provided with a
credential signed by the officers of the society or
council be represents, certifying to his appoint-
ment, such credential to be given up to the Secre-
tary, immediately on his arrival at the Con-
gress.
3. The time of meeting shall be as follows :
on the first day to assemble at 12 o'clock noon
prompt; on all other days at 9 30 am.; adjourn
at 1. re-assemble at 2, and adjourn at 6 o'clock
each day.
-

4. The roll shall be °idled promptly to time
morning and afternoon, the names of all dele-
gates late or absent to be read over with the
minutes each morning.

5, At the opening of the annual Congress, the
Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee shall
take the chair pro forma until the Congress has
elected its own President,

-
6. A committee of three shall bo elected to
examine the credentials, and report thereon to the
meeting.
-- -

-
7. The delegate shall then proceed to elect the
President of the Congrese, preference being given
to a delegate of the town whore the Congress io
being held.

B..Tlee Congress shall then elect a Secretary, a
like preference being given.
9. The Congress Shall then elect a vice-Presi-
dent, a door-keeper and a messenger.
10. A standing committee of five shall then be
elected, to whom. shall be remitted the whole
business of the C6ngress ; the order of and subjects
for discussion, together with the whole financial
arrangements of the Congress. The.vice-president
to be the chairman of the committee.
11. After the routine business of election of
officers and committee, the president shall formally
open the Congress with an address.
12. The standing committee, with a view to
securing a proper despatch of business, with perfect
fairness to all who have been to the trouble to
prepare papers, of which due notice has been
given, shall have power to divide the Congress
into sections, so that those specially interested in
any particular question may have the fullest
opportunity for its discussion.
13. The standing committee shall be allowed to
retire at 4 o'clock eaeh day (one hour before
closing the sittings of Congress), for the purpose
of selecting and arranging the next day's pro-
gramme.
14. Each delegate shall pay to the treasurer, on
the first day of his arrival, the sum of 10s. towards
the expenses of the Congress; and in case he
represents more than one society, 10e. for every
such society he is delegated to represent. The
names of those who have, and those who have not
paid, to be read over when the roll is called on the
following morning. No person shall be deemed a
member of Congress until his levy is paid.
15. Tho reader of a paper shall be allowed
twenty minutes; the mover of a resolution fifteen
minutes; succeeding speakers ten minutes. each ;
no one shall speak more than once on any one
question. After the reply, no one shall be allowed
to speak on the question before the chair, but it
'shall be at once put to the vote by the chairman.
16. No second amendment, or rider to an ori-
ginal proposition, shall be put to the vote until
the first amendment is disposed of.
17. The voting shall be by show of hands; but '
in case of a dispute, the chairman may order a
division.
18. Two tellers shall be appointed by the Con-
gross, and their ruling shall be final.
19. If more than one amendment is proposed,
the standing committee may retire, together with
the 'movers of the resolution and amendments, for
the purpose of trying to secure unanimity, by
blending the amendments in such a manner as will
be most conducive to the harmony of Congress
and the despatch of business.
20. No delegate shall be allowed to read a
second paper until after all other papers' of which
notice has been previously given, have been read,
unless by special permission and sanction of the
standing committee, and the formal consent of
Congress.
21, In the selectioo of papers to be read, pre-
ference shall be given to those of which notice has
been given, and in the order in which they have
been received by the committee.
22. Subjects having special reference to the
trade of the town or locality where the Congress
is being held, shall in no case be allowed to oc-
cupy the time of more than one sitting of the
congress. 'And it is desirable that these special
subjects be laid before the committee as early as
practicable, for the purpose of arranging them
under one or two general heads, and embodying
them in one or two simple propositions.
23. No delegate shall leave the room without
the consent of the Vice-President: and delegates
absent one whole sitting without leave of absence,
shall be named by the Chairman.
24. A General or Parliamentary Committee of
nine. shall be elected on the last day of each Con-
gress, who shall continue in office until they
are re-elected, or their successors arc apPointed.
They shell elect from among themselves a
President, Treasurer, and Secretary for the
ensuing year; and they also shall remain in
office until they are re-elected, or their successors
are appointed.
25. All surplus monies, after payment of the
expenses of the Congress, shall be handed over to
the Treasurer of the Parliamentary Committee for
the general purposes of such Committee.
26. The duties of the Parliamentary Com-
mittee shall be (1) to watch all legislative
measures directly affecting the questions of labour,
and (2) to initiate, whenever necessary, such
legislative action as Coegress may direct, or as the
exigencies of the time and circumstances way
demand.
27. The officers, under the direction of the
committee, shall have authority to solicit sub-
scriptions, donations, or levies, for the purpose of
defraying the expenses incurred by such com-
mittee; but the mode of payment shall be left
optional with each society as to whether it shall
pay by levy or donation.
28. The Congress having been formally opened
by the President, after the usted routine business
of electing officers and committee, the Parlia-
!limitary Committee shall present their report for
the past year, which shall be read by the Parlia-
mentary Secretary, and shall lay it on the table
for discussion by the Congress.
29. The Parliamentary Committee shall assist
and co-operate with the local committee of the
town where the next Congress is to be hold, for
the purpose of making the arrangements as com-
plete as possible and preparing the questions to
be discussed, anStogether to take such joint action
as the business or other special circumstances of
the time may render necessary or desirable.
30. The Parliamentary Commi!tee, in conjunc-
tion with the local committee, shall be empowered
to invite persons to attend the sittings of the Con-
gress whose presence they may deem Enlvisub!e
and desirable such persons to be allowed to
address the desirable,
